Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair I desire to draw the attention of the right hon. First Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) to the return which was brought down to the House the other day as to the number of railway accidents which have occurred in the Dominion of Canada during the past six months, and the enormous attendant loss of life. The return bi ought down covers the period from the first of October last to the first of April, and during that period of six months no less than 142 accidents took place in which, or as a result of which, 179 human lives were lost. It is a matter profoundly to be regretted that even since the first of April there have been other railway accidents. Several have occurred since that time in which, or as a result of which, many human lives have been lost. There seems to have been an epidemic, if I may use the expression, of accidents during the past eight or nine months. From the information obtained from the government, it appears, Mr. Speaker, that there is no public official under the control of the Department of Railways and Canalg, or of the Minister of Labour, whose duty it is to make inquiry at once into the cause which has led to these accidents, to make inquiry under oath to ascertain all the particulars antecedent and leading up to an accident, to ascertain any steps that might be taken to avoid a recurrence of a similar accident, to ascertain what was the condition of the road bed and rolling stock, to make inquiry as to the number of hours employees on these railways are on duty, to make inquiry as to the efficiency of the train crew, as to the sufficiency of the station help, as to the hours the station masters are supposed to be at work, and also to make inquiry as to the experience and
efficiency of the telegraph operators. I think it must appeal to hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House that in view of the number of accidents that have happened during the past six months in the conduct of our railways and in view of the fact that these railways are operated under a code of rules which have to be submitted to and approved by the government it is in the public interest that some official should be appointed at once by the government and given full oower to make ino.uiries as to these accidents and to endeavour to ascertain their causes and put a stop to their recurrence in the future. We learned recently from the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals that there was no official whose duty it was to make such an inquiry. At present, all the information that the public obtain as to the cause of an accident, is gleaned from the finding of the coroner's jury, but I am sure I am within the sense of this House when I say that these juries do not obtain all the information that is necessary for the public to form a judgment as to the causes which have led to the accident. It seems to me that there is something wanting in the method adopted by coroners' juries to obtain this information. It seems to me that it is necessary in the public interest that an official should be appointed to make these inquiries, not only that a more searching investigation may be made into the causes of accidents, but also that the employees of the company who may be called to give evidence may have the protection which such an official could afford them in giving evidence before a jury or making a statement to him. I believe that in the United Kingdom there is some public official whose duty it is when a serious railway accident occurs involving a loss of human life to proceed at once to the scene of the accident, make a full and complete inquiry and report to the government. I am sure it is so self evident that it is desirable to have an inquiry of this kind instituted and a report made to the government that I only need to draw the attention of the right hon. First Minister and of h?s colleagues of the government to the situation which exists in Canada,, to have them take definite action in this matter at the earliest possible moment. We have the Department of Railways and Canals and we have also a Department of Labour. It would surely be the function of an official of one or other of these departments to act in the manner suggested. I believe that the Department of Labour has an official whose duty it is to inquire into the number of hours, work performed, the wages paid, and so on, on works with which the government is identified. I think under these circumstances the powers of this officer might be enlarged, or some officer might be appointed from the Department of Railways and Canals to make an investigation such as I have suggested and to make a report. I saw it stated in one
JCOMMOjSTS
of the English papers recently that during the year 1902, notwithstanding the many millions of passengers carried by railways in the United Kingdom, not one human life was lost. It is deplorable and regrettable that the public of Canada have had to read from day to day and month to month during the past six or eight months of accideut succeeding accident with daily regularity and with attendant loss of life and property. I think if such an officer as I have suggested were appointed the result would probably be greater care upon the part of all concerned in the management and operation of railways. Railway companies have been given great privileges and great powers; they ought to be held responsible by the people for the way in which these privileges and powers are exercised, and it seems to me that if a rigid inquiry were made wnen-ever an accident occurs in which human life is lost, and if those responsible were held strictly accountable for the loss of human life, much greater care would be exercised than at present in the operation of these roads, and the result would be that in future we would have fewer accidents and less loss of life. I ask the Prime Minister or the Minister of Railways and Canals, or the Postmaster General or whatever minister is to answer :	What is the
policy of the government with respect to this matter ? Has the attention of the government been called to these frightful accidents which are growing constantly more frequent from one end of the country to the other ? Is it the intention of the government to take some decisive action to have an inquiry on oath as to the cause of these accidents ? Is it the intention of the government to hold the company responsible, or the employees responsible, if dereliction of duty is shown ? I am sure, Sir, that the matter is of sufficient importance to justify me in drawing the attention of the House to it at the present time. I know that the people throughout the country are commencing to fear very much, are in fact becoming nervous because of the frequency of these accidents.

I have no complaint to make at all that my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) has brought the subject up this afternoon. He was good enough to drop me a note a few moments ago telling me that he would call attention to it when the House would go into Supply.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair).

speechtext: I did not expect the House to go into Supply for some hours yet.

I understand. Had I had a little more time it would have enabled me to bring down some information which might have a bearing upon the subject, but perhaps a subsequent opportunity may offer. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) is no doubt irn-
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
pressed, as others have been, with the extreme gravity of this subject. It is startling to think that so many lives have been lost in railway accidents within the short period of six months, and unless we had the actual figures one would have scarcely thought it possible. Immediately these ' facts were brought to my notice I submitted the subject for the consideration of my colleagues, and we have been considering it since at every spare moment which has been available to us. We are considering very seriously what is the best course for us to take. It has not escaped our attention, and I can assure my hon. friend that we are not indifferent in the matter. But it is a much easier thing to say that action should be taken than to determine upon the nature of the details of such action. In my own department there was an accident recently which it was possible for me to deal with without getting formal authorization from the Governor in Council, and I confess that I have not yet been able to find an individual possessing the precise qualifications that would be necessary to enable him to conduct such an inquiry in an efficient manner. You need a man who has practical experience in the operation of railways, who is familiar at least with the regulations in a general way, and who knows from having worked on railroads in what manner these accidents are likely to occur, so that he can press his investigation in the most effective way. ITp to this time I have not been able to select a person who I think possesses the necessary qualifications for that purpose. The Railway Act contains ample power to authorize the Governor in Council to appoint an officer and to endow him with any powers which may be necessary for the purpose of conducting a thorough inquiry; authorizing the summoning of witnesses, the compelling of them giving testimony, the production of hooks, papers and documents, and all evidence that may throw light upon the question. I think the present legislation is ample in that respect. However, I would point out that that law has been on the statute-book for a very' long number of years, ever since confederation, and it has never been acted upon so far as I am aware of. It may be that in a special case a person has been appointed to hold a particular individual inquiry, but there has been no oflicial named or charged with the duty of holding inquiries whenever accidents upon railways occur, entailing loss of life or of property. I appre-fiend that there have been very grave accidents in the past; as disastrous no doubt to life and property as any that have recently occurred, so that the subject must have been oftentimes under consideration, but for one reason or another no official has been appointed. I am not authorized definitely to say just what action the Governor in Council will take upon this subject, but the House and the country may rest assured that we will endeavour to reach a wise conclusion in the premises, and if it shall appear to

us that the appointment of an official for such a purpose would tend to produce good results, that course will be determined upon.
AVhat is the practice in the old country ?

There is an official in the old country who has general authority to make on his own motion inquiry into any railway accidents and to report his conclusions to the Home Office or to the Board of Trade, or to some department pf the imperial government. It may be that we would do well to have an official similarly equipped with power and appointed by the government of Canada. My hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) has alluded to the remarkable freedom from loss of life on railways in the old country. It is a very striking fact, but it does not mean that loss of life has not taken place to a very considerable extent in connection with the operation of railways. It merely refers to the fact that the lives of passengers have not been lost. The accidents referred to in the return brought down the other day are not accidents to passengers alone. A very small proportion of them involved loss of life to passengers on railway trains. We know, unfortunately, that some very serious casualties have occurred whereby passengers have lost their lives, but the great majority of deaths and permanent injury on railways occur in the shunting yards to employees, and not when the trains are on the line in the ordinary course of travel. The men get a carelessness bred by familiarity with the habit of jumping on and off shunting engines. They are fully alive to the danger and hazard of what they are doing when they are committing an indiscretion, but before they know what they are about, they are run over by a train and life is lost. So that it is not possible to organize any regulation which will protect the men to a complete extent, or to a much greater extent than the present regulations, against the consequences of their own negligence and folly. We had an accident of a grave character on the Intercolonial Railway the other day. one of the gravest that has occurred for a long time. It is almost impossible to form a judgment as to why or how that accident came about. I have had the very fullest reports from the officers of the department on the spot. There is no question at all but that every provision which has been ordained for the purpose of ensuring safety to trains coming and g pig which are liable to meet one another, had been observed, so far as regulations could do it. The conductors and engine men on both trains received their orders where the crossing of these two trains took place -at Windsor Junction: and they both acknowledged receiving them. The train which is entirely to blame for the collision came to the point at Windsor Junction where it ought to have stopped. There was the semaphore signal forbidding that train going out; yet, notwithstanding that the engine driver swept through, and within two miles and a half of where he should have stopped his train, it collided with the other.,
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: How long was that engineer on duty ?

Only three or four hours ; he had just come fresh to his train. That officer was one of the best and most experienced men we had ; he had been thirty-two or thirty-three years in the service without a mark against him. It appears that he did not lose Ms life, and he has made the statement that he must have lost his senses, which is the only explanation he can make. He knew he was to stop, and was apparently thoroughly alive to the duty of his stopping the train until he came near to the point where it was to stop, and then the mental machinery failed to work. Now, I do not think, if we had an investigation of the fullest and amplest character, it would give us any more evidence as to the facts : but I thought it was desirable, and I concluded that if I could find some suitable person who would go there and have everybody who knew anything at all about the matter give his evidence, I would have the matter thoroughly looked into. I do not know that we can get any more light, but it will be a satisfaction to know that every effort has been made to trace out all the facts and to see whether there is any fact that we do not know. I can only say to my hon. friend that we realize the full gravity and importance of this subject. We shall not treat it with indifference, hut will deal with it in such a manner as we deem | conducive to the protection of life and property.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am sure the members of the House will be gratified to know, from the statement of the lion. Minister of Railways and Canals, that the government have under consideration this very serious matter to which my hon. friend from West Toronto (Sir. Clarke) lias referred. I was somewhat surprised a few days ago to learn that the government had not in their possession any statistics of the number of fatal accidents that occur on railroads, or the number of persons injured in railway accidents.
We are providing for that in the new Bill.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I was going to suggest that the matter might be covered in the new Bill. The Minister of Railways and Canals has announced that under the law as it exists a person can be appointed to make an inquiry into an accident. In the past the public has been ignorant except in the case of fatal accidents, as to the cause of railway accidents, or where the responsibility rested.

It seems to me that we have arrived at a time in this country when the government should obtain under the Railway Act all the powers that are necessary, if they do not at present possess them, to investigate railway accidents, and also to see that the railway companies carry out the rules and regulations which are submitted to the government for approval. I am informed that sometimes there is a laxity in carrying out these rules and regulations, through overwork, the great pressure of traffic, and that sort of thing. I think it is the duty of the government to inquire into all these matters. However, I am very pleased to learn that the government have this subject under consideration, and all I would urge is that they try to put some machinery into operation as soon as possible with the view of minimizing and diminishing railway accidents, and somewhat approaching the state of perfection that exists in Great Britain, where my hon. friend states that during the year ending March 31st, 1902, there was not a single fatal railway accident.
Among the passengers.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The memorandum which is taken from the newspapers, does not say that, but I accept that as correct.

I do not think there is so much fault to be found with the rules of the companies. I do not think the trouble lies there, but it is due to the management of the railways doing their utmost to cut down their operating expenses. To this end they discharge old reliable men and put into their places younger and inexperienced men. The cause lies in that more than in anything else. When freight becomes congested it takes the trains longer to pass over the lines, and the men are kept longer on duty. As a result of being a long time on duty accidents occur due to that reason, the employees not being as alert as they would be if they worked only ordinary hours. I think the greatest curse of all is this system of cutting down expenses at the cost of efficiency. The loss of life, not only of employees but of the travelling public, is a result of the experimenting by railway companies to reduce the cost of operating their lines. I think that the government would take a step in the right direction if they would appoint some first-class man who, in case of accident, would have full power to fairly investigate. These investigations held by coroners' juries are not reliable and in many cases do not bring out the actual facts. As one having some railway experience, I am in a position to say that the despatches in railway offices frequently send orders which they refuse to O. K. If they carried out the rules of the company, they would O. K. these orders, but they have refused and what has been the result ? The result has been that when the operators at the

stations were asked to produce the O. K. they could not because the despatchers had refused to give it to them. So that an operator, although he had been doing his duty, had no proof to bring, because the despatcher refused to give the O. K. order. I know myself of a serious accident which was visited on a man who was perfectly innocent.

I would like to ask the Hon. Minister of Railways if he has taken any steps towards having an investigation generally into the frequency of these accidents during the past few months, and into the cause of the accident on the Intercolonial Railway ?

I have said that nothing has been done in the way of appointing any official to pursue inquiries of this kind since the law has been on the statute-book, and that although I have power as minister, in connection with the Intercolonial Railway, to have an investigation on my own motion without getting authority by Order in Council, into the accidents which occur on the Intercolonial Railway, none have yet been investigated except by officials in the ordinary way, but that I was quite resolved to have, if I could find a suitable person, an official appointed for that purpose in connection with the Intercolonial Railway. I further stated that I would have an investigation into the recent accident.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What I asked the hon. gentleman was whether he had taken any steps of any kind to investigate into the cause of the frequency of these accidents during the few past months. We have had a discussion in which it has been urged that the accidents are nearly always due to the desire of railway companies to reduce the cost of operating their lines, and I wish to know if any steps had been taken at any time, of any kind, to investigate into this matter.
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I am very glad to hear that the hon. Minister of Railways proposes to consider the question of making an inquiry through a proper official into the causes of accidents. This inquiry should not be made merely after an accident occurs but should be in the nature of a general and continuous inspection for the purpose of preventing accidents. I do not know, and I do not very much care to discuss whether the troubles we have had so frequently this year have been due to any one or more of the particular causes referred to in the House to-day. But whatever the cause, whenever a serious accident happens, you will find that there are turn or three officials of one class or another implicated, each of whom has neglected some rule or order of the company, and that if any one of them had observed the rules

and regulations approved by tbe government, the neglect of another would not have caused the accident. Nearly always you will find a combination of two or three errors causing an accident and that if one of the men had done his duty, no trouble would have occurred. I think that indicates a very general neglect to carry out the rules adopted by companies and approved by the government. Those who know anything about the railway rules are convinced that if they were observed, an accident would be almost impossible except from some defect of machinery or appliance. In nearly every case there are two or three officials, one checking the other, and if any ,^ie of them did his duty there would be no accident. The difficulty is rather this, that a man working year after year without anything happening, becomes convinced that some particular rule is not essential to the safety of the train, and he neglects complying with it, and of course, when no accident occurs, nothing is ever heard of the neglect of the rule. That is due to the very natural reluctance of one employee to peach on his fellow employee. The officials of the railway companies probably never hear of the neglect until some lives are lost, or there is some destruction of property. Then an investigation takes place, and they learn that for months, and perhaps for years, some particular rule never has been observed. The inspector, of which the bon. member for West Toronto has spoken, should be a man in continuous employment, and not one sent out simply when the minister hears of some dreadful accident. He should be on duty as inspector from the beginning of the year to the end, travelling continually over the railways and seeing that the rules provided for the safety of the public are being observed. If a competent official of that kind were appointed I am satisfied that many of these accidents would be avoided, and we would have less need for investigating the cause of destruction of life and property.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, I ask leave to say a few words on the subject of wrecks and loss of life upon the railways, which was under discussion before the House rose for recess. These disasters seem to haVe been especially frequent since the last of December; the losses since that time have been quite remarkable. It is time steps should be taken to prevent the continuance of this great evil. We are sent here by the people to represent the people and to protect them, and this is an occasion that calls for action on our part. We have before us. in the person of the hon. Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair) the
man who should take the first step in this matter. Of course, unless that hon. gentleman moves, other managers and presidents of railways will say : So long as the government remains inactive, we will do the same. And in so saying they will be quite right. The Minister of Railways is the proper man and the only man to set this reform in motion. We were told in 1890 that this government would be a government of reform and a government of example. Let the government set the example and bring forth a proper measure of reform. What I wish to say is this-for I will speak but a few moments and would like to be well understood-in the first place the Minister of Railways must be aware of how his own men are worked on the government railways. I cannot speak so well about the government railways, but speaking of railways that I do know, I can tell the House that drivers- engineers, as some call them, but they call themselves 1 drivers '-firemen, conductors and telegraph operators work too many hours at a stretch. Often, you see these men go on duty in the morning with instructions to remain on duty until they are told to quit. Sometimes they will be ten, twelve and even fifteen hours on duty. The result may be that a wreck takes place and there is a loss of life. And when the question is asked by the public how the accident occurred, they are told : It was on account of tiie operator. But there is somebody behind. and the operator is not always to blame. Those who give instructions to the operator are often to blame. When the men in responsible positions tell an operator or an engineer, or a conductor, to stay on duty until he is told to quit, they are the men who are to blame, and the only ones. The Minister of Railways, being at the head of the government in these matters, should make the first move, and provide that drivers, conductors, firemen and telegraph operators shall be allowed to work only so many hours out of the twenty-four. Understand me well-when I say they should be restricted to so many hours, I do not mean to say that you should go to the extreme. To say that one of these employees shall not work more than fourteen hours or sixteen hours would not do. Take a driver who runs an express at the rate of forty, forty-five or fifty miles an hour, and sometimes even at sixty miles an hour, at the risk of his life-such a man should not be on duty more than four hours at a time, say four out of sixteen or twenty. Working for such a length of time, these men will be fit, and it will be safe to entrust to them the lives of passengers. The same way with the conductors, and the same way with the telegraph operators. A telegraph operator, let us say, is ordered on at six o'clock in the morning; and at eight o'clock in the evening or nine or ten o'clock, his hours of duty not ended, he becomes tired and goes to sleep. A train may pass by which should be stop-

peel by the operator, but he, tired with overwork, is sound asleep, how can he stop the train 7 The result is that there is a wreck ahead and loss of life. The government may say that it will be too expensive to give these men short hours. But there are two ways of looking at it. Suppose that it should cost the government .$20,000 a year extra to employ the additional staff necessary to give this class of employees such short hours. Why, in one wreck you will lose fifteen or twenty or sixty or even a hundred thousand dollars. But that is not all, nor is it the worst. It may be that five or six or even ten or fifteen lives are lost. Who will restore those lives 7 The people are dead and gone and that is the last of them for this world. The Minister of Railways, if he would but say the word could prevent all this; and to him the people look to take the first step. And if the hon. minister is kind enough to adopt the necessary measures, he shall have my support. It will be the duty of everybody to support him cordially. I was coming up on the Canada Atlantic Railway to-day. Some people asked : Why do not you go by the Canadian Pacific Railway, for there is a strike on this road 7 There is one example. A number of employees have stopped work, and we are even told that signals have been ta mpered with. Of course, it may be said that the government is not to blame. But all this goes to show the dangers that are involved and that should be overcome as far as possible. My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Blair) must travel a great deal by the railways. Should he lose his leg in a railway accident-would not that be a loss that could not be made good to him by $50,000 ? And should he happen to lose his life, of course, there is no money that would redeem that. Therefore, this House has a right to call upon the hon. minister to take steps before more disasters occur, to secure greater safety to those who operate or travel by the railways.

Mr. Speaker, the subject which is before the House, and which was discussed for some little time before recess is of more than passing importance. It is one that has awakened keen and lively interest in the public mind. I am not at all in sympathy with the kind of propaganda which would unnecessarily excite the public mind against railway companies or unnecessarily embarrass those companies with legislative enactment. We know that the duties of railway managers are of a very onerous character. On one hand they have the lives of people committed to their care in very large numbers. On the other hand, they have the interest of the public who have invested their money in their railways, and the managers are naturally desirous of running their roads so that they may pay some decent dividend on the capital invested. It may be that there has been too great a tendency towards econ-Mr. MORIN.
omy in the running of railways, which may be to some extent responsible for the large number of accidents that have occurred in this country during the past six months. This is a matter of national interest and of national importance. It is not merely a question of loss to the railway companies, or even a question of a loss of life, but it is a matter of national importance, because if the statistics in Canada should show that life is much more imperilled on railways here than in other countries, it would be detrimental to the settlement of this country. it would be detrimental to the investment of capital in this country, and in a number of ways it would hinder that progress which we have a right to expect and which we are all looking for.	[DOT]
As I said before, I am not in favour of legislative enactments that would unnecessarily embarrass the operation and management of railways, but I think we owe it to the public and to our constituents to bestir ourselves and to prove that we are alive to the public interest in view of the deplorable loss of life that has recently occurred in railway accidents. I understand that the railway companies have very strict rules for their employees, which are intended to safeguard the travelling public, but these rules are not always implicitly obeyed. For instance, I understand they have very strict rules with regard to the use of intoxicants while their men are upon duty. Now from what I can gather from remarks that I have heard, I believe that in many cases the men are worked over hours, whether from compulsion or whether from a desire to work longer hours in order to get more pay. I do not know. But certain it is that evidence has come out to show that men have been kept on duty fifteen or sixteen hours in the twenty-four. Now it is not in human nature to bear up under such a strain, nor ought the lives of the travelling public to be committed to men who work such long hours. From what I can gather they resort to stimulants in consequence, and from information had I believe that engine drivers and their assistants are in the habit of using intoxicants to stimulate them under weariness and exhaustion in performance of arduous duties for long periods. I was recently with a man who said that he had frequent opportunities of riding upon one of the engines belonging to a line of railway that I know very well. He had been himself in the employment of the company, and he stated that having the confidence of the engine drivers he frequeptly rode with them, and he knew for a fact that they were accustomed to take stimulants with them, and were frequently under the influence of those stimulants. More than that, we know that men who work very long hours and become wearied have been known to fall asleep on their engines, when they were travelling at the rate of forty or fifty miles an hour. We can form but a slight conception of the immense danger to the travelling

public which must ensue when they have entrusted their lives to men in this condition and under these circumstances.
I understand that this motion has for its . object to bring this matter to the attention of the government so that some means may be taken to safeguard the travelling public and lessen the danger of railway accidents which have been so frequent recently. Compared with the record of European countries and compared with the record of Great Britain, our record for railway accidents, during the last six months especially, is of an unenviable character. I do not know how it compares, as to mileage and population, with the record in the neighbouring republic, where accidents have been considered more frequent than in any other part of the world. But I am sure we are acquiring an unenviable reputation in that respect.
I hope that this discussion will lead to some ! appointment by the government which will reassure the people, and will at least show that the government appreciate the importance of this matter. The railway companies have been given large privileges in their j charters, and we have a right to exercise supervision over their management by the appointment of some commission of inspection which will tend to lessen the frequency of accidents which have been so appalling during the last six months.

I think it proper to draw , the attention of the Minister of Railways and Canals to one branch of this case which, I think, judging from the remarks he made this afternoon, he has failed fully to appreciate. I refer to a feature of the case that was clearly brought out by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) and also by the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker), that is, the question of prevention rather than the question of investigation after the difficulty has arisen. I understand from watching what has happened in the last six months, and from taking note of the accidents that happened before that time, that there is a necessity for taking preventive measures, or such means of supervision being adopted as will lead to a diminution of the danger of accidents in the future. That this can be done, I think will be admitted by any person who has given any attention to the matter. When these accidents occur we have had evidence from time to time that in many instances they result, not from the want of stringent regulations made by the railway companies, but from the failure of the company to put those rules vigorously into operation. In many cases accidents have undoubtedly resulted from the fact that the companies were endeavouring to carry on their operations with too small an expenditure of money, or were imposing upon their employees more duties or greater responsibilities than they could possibly discharge. Now this afternoon the member for Hamilton, I think, referred to the fact that the railway companies, while they make regulations and obtain the proper sanction of those regulations, still in many instances have failed to carry them out. I know an instance that occurred between the town of Barrie and the city of Toronto not many months ago, where the regulation as to the passage of trains at a certain point had been deliberately ignored for, I think I am safe in saying, a year, if not to the direct knowledge of the head officials of the company, at all events to the knowledge of many of their prominent officials. While no trouble arose, they virtually winked at the infringement of their own rules. But, unfortunately, not long ago an accident occurred, and what then happened ? All the officials that could be charged with responsibility were immediately dismissed. The company would not take as an excuse that the company itself had long been aware that the rule was being broken. The answer was : You are bound to obey the rules, and when an accident occurs you must stand the consequence. This is only one instance of many which point to the fact which the Minister of Railways and Canals entirely ignored in the remarks he made this afternoon. What the public needs is the appointment of some official of the government whose duty it would be to see that proper regulations are made and enforced to insure the safety of the travelling public, to make himself familiar with the actual working of the various railways, and to see that these regulations are efficiently carried out. What the hon. minister says in regard to the fact that there is a statute in force which enables us to appoint some one to investigate the causes of accidents after the accidents have occurred indicates a very ineffective remedy, but if an active official of the government is charged with the duty of seeing from time to time that certain necessary rules are being carried out on the various railways, then, there is no doubt at all that great good will result and the number of accidents will be greatly diminished. This, I hope, will be sufficient to draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals to this important matter and to enable him to act and to act now. I cannot but feel that it is a very regrettable circumstance that whilst everybody in this country has been shocked by the number of accidents that have occurred, whilst every public man, every intelligent man, has had full knowledge for months and more than months of the absolute necessity of some action being taken by the government to lessen the number of fatal accidents that are occurring, the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals has not been in a position to-day to tell the House that he has adopted some effective measure already to advance the remedy and prevent the recurrence of these disastrous accidents.

Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Cimir to go into Supply, I would like to draw tlie attention of the House to what I consider a very reasonable grievance. We have now been sitting for a month and I think I am right-
I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) has spoken on the motion to go into Committee of Supply.
speakername: The POSTMASTER GENERAL (Hon. Sir William Mulock).

speechtext: No, I only asked a question.
Only a question V

We have been sitting for a month and I think I am right in saying that with the exception of some very trifling legislation, there has been very little done beyond the passing of estimates and the furnishing of supplies. In this I think we have acted very generously; we have voted, ii I mistake not, several million dollars and we have shown a disposition, at least every time I have been present in this House to go into Supply, and I think I may claim that we are doing it unduly at the present moment. I have no desire for my own part to retard in any way the work of Supply. I know that it involves considerable labour for the minister in charge of the department, and for my own part, in order to advance the work of the session, I want to assist the minister as much as possible when the estimates of his department come up to pass these estimates, because we have quite enough work without creating obstruction in the slightest degree. For my own part I disclaim any idea of creating obstruction, but what I would submit to you, Mr. Speaker, and to lion, members of both sides of the House respectfully is that we are not proceeding in the regular way. We have grievances to redress and the voting of supplies ought to be preceded by the redress of grievances. Now, I will just enumerate to the House some of the important questions that are before us this session and which, according to my view, create the question of grievance. I will not speak of the tariff, Mr. Speaker, because we have the announcement of the budget speech for to-morrow; still, I do not suppose there is throughout the whole country a single person, however indifferent that person may be to the great political issues of the day. who, if asked, what is the question that is disturbing the public most at present, or which is creating an interest in politics, will not answer at once : It is the question of the tariff. Well, we have been over a month here and we have had no opportunity for the discussion of this most important question upon which there are so many different opinions throughout the Dominion. We have remedies to apply to the Election Act. Hon. members

on this side, and lion, members on the other side of the House have introduced measures to remedy serious grievances in the electoral law. Why cannot we take up these grievances and remedy them before we continue voting money day after day as we are doing at present. At the very opening of the session we had the announcement of the Redistribution Bill. What is that but a grievance ? The right lion, leader of the government (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) said, when introducing his Bill, that it was intended by that Bill to remedy a grievance, hut going outside altogether of the question of party in respect to that Bill, the taking of (he census and the result of that census now before us creates a grievance and before proceeding any farther with Supply we should apply ourselves strictly and absolutely to remedy that grievance. That is what I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the House, in respect to the Redistribution Bill.
We have had the announcement made to the public and I think it was confirmed in this House that we are going to have a transportation commission. That was foreshadowed in the speech from the Throne. What is tlie scope of that commission ? Is it designed by that commission to remedy the serious ills that are indicated in the speech from the Throne. What will the work of the commission be ? Is it going to take away from the government and the House the mission of defining and establishing a policy upon that great question, perhaps the most momentous one we have to decide during the present session ? What will be the cost of the commission ? Is it a machinery which will meet with the approval of the House ? Why cannot we, in accordance with our constitutional duty, keep Supply back until these grievances have been set right ? Why cannot these questions be discussed before we get to work to vote the money required for the next year ? We have the Railway Bill; we have a voluminous document set before us, the object of which is to remedy a grievance. We have divided opinions as to the nature of the remedy afforded for existing ills. We have to discuss the question of the railway commission whether, here, again, that commission will undertake the responsibility of curing the evils which have been time and again set before the House by bon. members from the far west, by lion, members from the province of Ontario and from the other eastern provinces. We may be divided upon this question; we may be divided irrespective of the question of politics. but what I submit to the House and the government is that if we proceed regu-Iarly and constitutionally we ought to take up a measure like that one and see it through before we are called upon to vote supplies.
I believe there is to be a militia Bill ; we have had a foreshadowing of great reforms in our militia system which must entail

considerable public expenditure.' Our representatives at the conference in London stated what would be done in this respect when they returned to Canada. Where is that militia Bill ? Are the increased expenditures for these reforms to be brought in at the end of the session, or are we going to have them before proceeding to the duty which we must accomplish en connaissance de cause, when we are called upon to vote supplies for the coming year. Again there is the question of the new transcontinental line which has been discussed throughout Canada for many months passed, and yet all that we have heard with regard to this most important subject is what the newspapers have published of statements made by ministers outside of this House. We have heai'd nothing in this House which would indicate to us what extra expenditure will be laid on the public by reason of this great transportation problem. Is it unfair that we in our role as critics of the government, should ask that before we be requested to vote supplies that we should know what the nature of that measure is going to be. Should the House go into Supply to-night we will be asked to vote money for the building of wharfs, and the construction of breakwaters, and are we not entitled before we go into this voting of supplies to know what is the policy of the government in respect to that transcontinental scheme which will call upon the people of this country to make very great additional sacrifices of money ? After all, under the modern understanding of the constitution, the government is nothing else than a committee of this House, and the government should make known to this House its policy on such an important matter as this. I was through a by-election just before this session opened, and one of the important questions discussed there was the reorganization of the departments of the government. The electorate of Mai-sonneuve were told that if the Department of Public Works had been taken from the province of Quebec where it had been for many years, it was with a good object. It was stated that in view of the great works which are to be executed on the lower St. Lawrence, it might be better that the Department of Public Works should remain vested in one who knew the immediate requirements of the navigation of the lower St. Lawrence, and we were told by the ministers there, as we have been told in the speech from the Throne that a Bill would be introduced which would place in the hands of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries the control of the works on the St. Lawrence from Montreal to the sea. Where is that measure ? If it was a grievance during the election in Maisonneuve it is a grievance still. Is it right that we should be asked to vote money for public works before an attempt is made to remove that, grievance as the government promised it 43
would be made ?, There is also a Bill, which has the character of a public Bill, to change the constitution of the Supreme Court. That Bill is in the hands of my hon. friend from St. Jean and Iberville (Mr. Demers). I venture to assert that the hon. gentleman is ready to proceed with that Bill which he claims is destined to remedy a grievance, but I venture also to assert that the hon. gentleman has been requested to leave that Bill in abeyance, just as he has been requested to leave in abeyance the Bill designed to remedy what we in my province consider a grievance, namely the existing state of the law as interpreted by the highest tribunal in the empire in regard to the protection of private property from fire caused by the operation of railways. All these and many other important matters involving questions of policy, questions of grievance, are put aside and this House is asked, to go into the voting of supplies. Under these circumstances it is not only our right but it is our duty to call attention to this state of affairs. Unless we have some absolute assurance from the government as to the policy which is going to obtain in regard to these great questions, which are really the questions of the session, we will righteously incur the blame of the people of Canada for consenting to this unconstitutional method of conducting public business, and when we have voted supplies, then we will be left without any adequate remedy to insure the removal of public grievances. I protest against this manner of conducting public business. We have seven or eight important questions ; the only questions of the session that really interest the public, and the constitutional and proper method for us to pursue is first and foremost to apply ourselves to the solution of these questions and then take up the voting of supplies. I say this frankly to the government. I have no desire to obstruct business in any way ; it is not in accordance with my feelings to be compelled to have recourse to the system of discussing at length! item after item. But it seems to me, Sir, that we are varying the good old rule of the British parliament that first and foremost we must proceed with the settlement of measures which are for the good of the people and for the settlement of which we are here, and that we should keep back the furnishing of the supplies until those measures are satisfactorily settled. Having said this, if the government call upon us to proceed with supply this evening, I am quite ready as I was when we were called on to go into supply several weeks ago to go on; but I felt that I would not be performing my duty if I did not call your attention, Sir, and the attention of the House to what I consider an important point.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have



the assurance of my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) that his observations are simply based on a deep conviction on his part as to what should be the procedure rather than upon any desire to delay the legitimate work of parliament; but he has to-night laid down a new practice, and one without a parallel either in the mother of parliaments or in the parliament of Canada. I have yet to learn that it has' become a practice, either by rule or by practice itself, that parliament shall not proceed with the great work of the session in such order as may be most convenient for the government and parliament and most in the interests of the country. It has never yet been the rule that great public measures introduced by the government shall always be disposed of before the voting of supplies. My hon. friend has perhaps forgotten the advanced state of work when parliament met this session. I have had twenty years or more of experience in this House, and I think I am correct in saying-and every hon. member who has been in parliament during that time, will agree with the statement-that never before did a government meet parliament better prepared with its work than did the government at the present session. When the speech from the Throne was disposed of-and it was disposed of with gratifying business alacrity-the departmental reports were immediately laid on the Table, and we were prepared to render an account of our administration during the last fiscal year. A few days afterwards we laid before parliament some of the important legislative measures now engaging the attention of the country. On the Order paper I find, among government Bills and Orders. Bill No. 21 an Act to amend the law respecting railways. My hon friend would argue that we must dispose of that measure before we proceed with Supply. Is that his argument ? That Bill was introduced on the 20th of March. It is of a very far-reaching character. No goveniment ever introduced a measure of this kind into the parliament of Canada before; it affects great interests; it is a measure the country is greatly interested in. Does it not seem becoming that the details of that measure should be a reasonable time before the country before parliament proceeds to convert it into an Act of parliament ? We do not possess all the wisdom of the country-
Hear, hear.

I include hon. gentlemen opposite in that observation. The aggregate wisdom of parliament itself does not perhaps represent all the wisdom of the country; and I hope that before that measure becomes law many of the citizens of Canada who are deeply studying it will offer valuable suggestions towards its betterment, if it is not perfect already. Is it not becoming that a measure Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
of such importance, and one so novel in its character in this country at least, and which relates to the interests of every class in the Dominion should not be proceeded with with undue haste ? My hon. friend complains that we are not proceeding to improve the harbour of Montreal or the river St. Lawrence. I find by the estimates that my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works is about to ask parliament to assent to a vote of $500,000 for the improvement of the St. Lawrence ship channel. This is not a new work, but one to which parliament has already committed itself. My hon. friend complains that we are not proceeding with the improvement of the St. Lawrence channel, and yet he will not let us get into committee in order that we may vote the money required for that purpose. He argues that this work must stand over and that we must not go into Committee of Supply until we dispose of these important Bills, including the Bill for the establishment of a railway commission. I ask this House is it the right procedure to stop the voting of supplies until we pass that Bill ? Have we all the wisdom that the country possesses on that measure ? Would we not be chargeable with proceeding with undue haste if now, at the conclusion of the first month of the session, and before the Bill has been before the public twenty days, we took it from the people and converted it into an Act of parliament to-night ?
Practically the same Bill was introduced last session and has been before the country ever since.

Then it will be all the better for the careful consideration it has had during that time. Then my hon. friend argues that we should proceed with the budget speech before we vote the supplies. The budget speech is fixed for to-morrow. Was a budget speech ever presented at an earlier date ? I trust it will be an exceedingly gratifying one to hon. gentlemen, as I think it will be to the country; and inasmuch as that speech is to be delivered in a very few hours from now, what public good would be gained by deferring the public business to-night and idling the time of parliament ? Hon. gentlemen will remember that this is not government day. This is a private members' day, and I think I am correct in saying that never before in twenty years has the Order Paper been as free of matters introduced by private members as it is at this moment. We were able, with the common consent of parliament, to take Thursday as a government day, simply because private members' work had been exhausted, and to-day, before six o'clock was reached, all the private members' work was exhausted, we had the option of adjourning or proceeding with government business. As a working government we deemed it our duty to do our work instead of adjourning at six

o clock. My hon. friend complains that we should stop the voting of supplies until the hon. member for St. John and Iberville (Mr. Demers) proceeds with two measures, forgetting that these two measures were called for this afternoon and were not proceeded with. Consequently the Order paper was exhausted and we had the option of adjourning or taking^ ifp Supply. I think the country will admit that we are pursuing the right course when we proceed with the business of the country. My hon. friend complains that we are not going on with the Redistribution Bill, and he claims that till we do, Supply should not be voted. But the Redistribution Bill has been referred to a special committee. Does my hon. friend say that the whole proceedings of parliament should stand over, that nothing should be done, that Supply should not be voted until the committee on the Redistribution Bill have made their report ? It is only necessary to mention my hon. friend's suggestion to show how absurd it is. My hon. friend is in a hurry to see a new transcontinental railway policy introduced. But how long did it take the former parliaments to formulate a policy for the transcontinental road we now have, the Canadian Pacific Railway ? Was that policy introduced at as' early a period in the session as the present V This scheme of a new transcontinental road is a large one. It would have far-reaching importance. It has been discussed in the public press, and many different opinions have been advanced. The hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) not long ago advocated the construction of such a road by the government, other hon. members favour giving aid to a private company to build it, and others protest against the adoption of any such policy at all. My hon. friends from St. Mary's division, Montreal (Hon. Mr. Tarte) and Pontiac (Mr. Murray) argue that the most important feature of transportation which can engage the attention of the country is not a transcontinental railway, but a canal connecting the Georgian Bay waters with the Ottawa river. All these different views and considerations must be well weighed before the government can be called on to decide on a policy. Yet my hon. friend argues that all these measures must be disposed of before we go into Supply, and supposing the government should say that it was not in favour of any of these policies, then, according to my hon. friend's argument, no Supply should be voted and the King's business should be allowed to fall into confusion. Our practice hitherto has always been that Supply should take up the time at the disposal of the government for that purpose on every government day, and on private members' days the time not required for private business. We are economizing time by proceeding in this way. It has never been the practice in any parliament to do what my hon. friend suggests, and I think that before this parliament inaugurates a new policy and procedure, it 43J
should take a little more time to consider it than can be had in this off-hand way of giving advice just on a motion to go into Supply. My hon. friend was not here when we adjourned last night or he would know that the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule), who was then leading the opposition, asked what business would be taken up to-day, and my right hon. colleague, the Prime Minister, announced that we would proceed with the Orders of the Day and if time were still left, we would take up the Public Works estimates. With regard to those estimates, let me point out that they do not involve any new public works, but are merely for the carrying on of public works, to which the country has already committed itself, and I am sure that my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier will see that whatever force his contention would'have if we were invitiug the House to vote expenditures on entirely new works, it can have no application when we are simply asking the House to deal with public works to which parliament has long since given its sanction.
Does the hon. minister apply that remark to the Quebec estimates ?
I am speaking of the Public Works estimates we are about to proceed with.

The pyrotechnical display which the hon. gentleman who is now leading the House has just given us, may have been interesting to the hon. gentlemen on that side, but it did not throw much new light on the situation. The hon. minister started out by saying that my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier was introducing some new principles. What new principles ? The principle he enunciated is as old as the British parliament, and that is the redress of grievances before Supply is granted. The hon. minister says that we have an important Bill before us, the Railway Commission Bill, a new measure, and that it has been before us for twenty-five days, but that measure, as he was reminded by an hon. member from this side, is only the Bill revamped which was before the House last year. It has been discussed by the press at different times throughout the year, but we have no substantial information from the government as to how that commission will be organized, what it will apply to when organized, what will be the scope of its powers, how it is likely to prove beneficial in redressing the grievances under which our people are labouring or in improving the transportation problem. These are questions on which the government has given practically no information. Is it improper that we should desire information as to the policy of the government on this important measure before we vote Supply ? No doubt it would suit the government to have the Supply voted as early as possible, because once the Supply Bill is passed the

government can dispense with our services. But it is for the puipose of having public measures considered as they should be, that the supplies are held back until we know the details of the government's policy and the lines of action they propose to carry out. The government have not given us that information. True they have announced their measures, but they are all like the Redistribution Bill, practically in blank form. The House has as yet no information as to how redistribution will take place. We are told that it is to be regulated by a committee, and the right hon. the First Minister has said to us :	1 When we appoint the committee we will hand in our schedule and you will do the same with yours.' And then, forsooth, we are likely to vote through ours whether you like it or dislike it. We are told that this is practically representation by population, but we are told in the next breath that county lines are to be observed. If you have one, you. cannot have the other. That was clearly pointed out years ago by the late Rt. Hon. Sir John A. Macdonald. He declared it was impossible to have representation by population if you observe the county lines. But you have the anomaly in this House that the government is going to observe county lines and yet is going to grant representation by population.
Are you opposed to the observance of county lines V

I am not saying whether I am opposed to it or not. I am simply showing what the information the government has given us about it, and expressing our desire to know more. Then, there is another very important question mentioned by my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) in which the country is vitally interested and on which we have no information. I refer to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. There are two or three transcontinental lines before the government and the country to-day, yet we are in the dark as to the policy the government intend to adopt with regard to them. We desire information. we wish to know what the government's policy is so that we may be able to judge for ourselves whether it is right to grant them these supplies or not. But, after we have granted these supplies, they may turn to us and say: You may go home we have the supplies and do not care for your opinions on other matters. This is the reason why we wish to know their policy with regard to these great matters now under discussion, before we grant them these supplies. The Commission Bill I have already referred to. It is a very important one, but wo know nothing yet as to what its scope is to be, what the powers of the commission will be, what railways the measure will apply to or how far it is likely to be useful to the railways or to the country. From the very first it seems

to have been the aim of the government to get the supplies voted. The hon. member for North York (Hon. Sir William Mulock) upbraids my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) with being unwilling to vote the supplies necessary for the works in the great port of Montreal. Why, last session we voted supplies for this work up to the 30tli of June next. The government have money enough to go on with, and there is plenty of time between now and the 30tli of June to vote any supplies that may be needed for the ensuing fiscal year. So, no question arises as to whether it is right or wrong to prevent the government from getting the supplies at the present time. My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) in my judgment was entirely right ; the position he takes is in harmony with the well understood principles of constitutional government. He only asks that the government should place their policy before parliament and before the country so that the opposition may have an opportunity of criticising it, and the country an opportunity of understanding it, before supplies are voted to enable them to carry on the affairs of the country. That is the position that has always been taken by parliament, and we are only doing our duty to parliament and the country, when we demand to know what the government's policy is on these various lines, before we grant them the supplies they are asking for.

Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.
Public works-chargeable to Income, harbours and rivers-Ontario-Bowmanville, to complete repairs to breakwater, $1,000.
Is this work on private property ?
I find that parliament has been expending money on this for a number of years. The property was originally vested in the municipality, I believe.
speakername: The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS (Hon. James Sutherland).

speechtext: Is it in private hands now?
I believe it is the property of private individuals.

It would be interesting to have the names of the owners of the property. Some of the hon. minister's supporters may be able to give us the information. It is extraordinary to vote public money to be spent on private property. The hon. minister ought to give us other information.

I only investigated the matter to-day, and was somewhat surprised to find that parliament was spending a good deal of money from time to time on some of these harbours that are not vested in the Crown. I must say, that although I have been in the House for a long time, I was not aware that this was so generally the custom as I find it to

have been. I And that there has been a total expenditure of $29,000 on this work by the Dominion government covering a number of years. So, this is not extraordinary, I may say. My hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) has taken part, like other members of the House, in voting more or less to this work. There was a vote of $4,000 last session, and this is a vote of only $1,000 to complete the work.

I understand that it was only to-day that the hon. minister became aware of the fact that this was private property. Would it not be as well to give the hon. minister an opportunity to further pursue his researches, and, for this purpose, to let this item stand for three or four days? He may be able, within that time, to get fuller information as to the owners of this property on which public money is being expended.

I am willing to give the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) all the information at my command.
I understand -that this property is mainly in the name of a Mrs. Raines, a widow of Montreal.
Is Sirs. Raines the sole proprietress ?
Almost the sole proprietress. There are other small shareholders.
Who are they ?
A part of the stock is held by a widow lady in Bowmanville, a Sirs. Galbraith, and another of the proprietary is Sirs. McClellan.

Are we to understand that the sole proprietors are these two widow ladies ?
The S1INISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. Three. And there are other very small stockholders.
The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) says that he can give us all the information. Will he not tell us who are the others in addition to these three widows ?

I do not pretend to have this information in the department. That which I have given, I have obtained from the member for the riding (Mr. Beith). This vote is only a small balance of $1,000 to complete the work.
A sort of a widow's mite.

It is very interesting and amusing, no doubt, to see the bachelor Slin-ister of Public Works looking after the interests of the widows. Of course, he would be reluctant to interfere with them. But there is involved in this vote a principle, a principle we have fought against for many years. We fought against it in the case of a dock at Sault Ste. Slarie, in the case of
another dock at Port Arthur, and, I think, in the case of a dock at Bruce Mines, and others. That principle is the expenditure of public money upon private docks. Some of these docks we have had to buy from their owners at high prices, and in buying, we had not even the advantage of a reduction in the price to the extent of the money we had put into them. That is where the principle comes in, a principle which, in my judgment, is entirely wrong, namely, to put public money into private docks which we may afterwards be obliged to buy, and to pay a higher figure for than their actual value.

Is this harbour owned by the government, and is the hon. member for West Durham looking after it and constituting himself the guardian of the three widows, owners thereof ? How much money has been spent there ?
Is the government taking over the Oshawa harbour ?
Yes.
How much money has been expended on it ?

I have not got that information at the moment.
BrontS, harbour improvements, $2,700.
Last year there was an appropriation of $3,000, most of which has been expended. This appropriation will complete the work.

Right away.
