speechtext:
I ask this question because the Postmaster General, a few minutes ago, stated that if we blocked the estimates we blocked the carrying on of the improvements. Last session we voted all the money that the government asked for up to the 30th of June, and we do not block any improvements in this country if we pass the estimates before the 30th of June. I understand that this money is not available until after the 30th of June of the present year, therefore the statement of the Postmaster General was altogether incorrect when he told my horn friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) that if we blocked supply in any way we blocked the improvements of Montreal harbour, because there was in the estimates of the Minister of Public Works a large amount for improvements in Montreal

harbour, and that money cannot be touched until after the 1st of July.

I think my hon. friend misunderstood the Postmaster General. What he said was that the appropriation the House was being asked for was to continue works that parliament had already authorized. My hon. friend is perhaps technically right in saying that this money cannot be spent until after the Supply Bill has been assented to. But he will remember that it is one of the misfortunes of conducting public works that if time is lost, if we are compelled to wait before beginning them, they may cost considerably more. After this vote passes it is quite within the right of the department to go on with the work. After parliament has assented to these votes, although the Supply Bill may not have passed, where the works are under contract, we feel ourselves authorized to go on and spend the money.
Was the $3,000 voted last year expended ?
Yes, $2,875 was expended up to the end of the year. The work was done by a government dredge.

This work has been going on for several years. I would like to ask the minister if the $2,700 now asked is likely to complete the dredging and the construction of the wharf, or will a further sum be required another year ? I may say that the people there are anxious to have this work fully completed, and I hope the minister will be able to tell us that the appropriation now asked for will complete the work.

The estimate submitted by the chief engineer is that $1,500 will complete the repairs to the pier, that $1,200 more is required for dredging the harbour to a depth of eight feet. He estimates that this will complete the work for the present.
So that no further sum will be required after the present year ?
Not for the present work.

Whilst this estimate is before us, there is another matter I would like to draw attention to. I regret that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is not in his place. It is to be regretted that whilst these estimates for public works are going through that that hon. gentleman should continually absent himself from the House, because there is so much connection between the two departments. I understand these wharfs are usually handed over to the Marine Department, that lighthouses are constructed by the Marine Department, so that there is a certain connection between the work done by the Public Works Depart-1 Mr. TAYLOR.
meut and that done by the Marine Department. Now, we have no person here to answer for the Marine Department. I drew the attention of the minister a year ago, I think, to the fact that the people were promised, in 1900, that a lighthouse would be constructed on this wharf. Such a construction would be very desirable. There is a considerable amount of fishing done on the lake extending some ten or fifteen miles from this port, and a lighthouse would be very desirable for the benefit of the fishermen. Sometimes in dark nights the men lose their way, and they have no signal to guide them to the port. If the department did nothing more than construct a lighthouse, it would be a great benefit. I was told last year, I think, that the government had no record of the promise that was made for the construction of a lighthouse. I can understand that. I think the promise was only made by the candidate who opposed me for the purpose of securing a few extra votes. I do not suppose he had the authority of the government, nor do I suppose that he lias any intention of seeing that the promise is carried out. But the promise was made to these people, and I am one of those who believe that every election promise of that kind ought to be carried out. In the case of Bowmanville, a public building was promised in the last by-election, when it was announced in the papers. 'Vote for Mr. Beith and you will have a public building.'
He denies that.

There is no necessity for denying it, it was published in the press at the time. The government did supplement the promise made to the electors at that time, when they were asked to vote for Mr. Beith and secure a public building ; and I think it is only fair that the government should supplement the promise made to the electors in the present case. The electors gave my opponent a good vote there, a great many more than he was entitled to. They have done their share of the contract, they have done their part, and now they want the job completed. I hope the Minister of Public Works will see that this work is given to them that they were promised.
I say again, I regret that the Minister of Marine is not in his place. It is important that he should be here whilst these estimates are going through, so that we may get some statement from him about it, because, apart from all other considerations, whether it was intended to be done at the time or not, or whether it was merely to influence an election, I say there is a necessity for it, and it will be in the public interest to erect it. I hope the hon. Minister of Public Works will be able to influence the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, if he has not the power within himself, to supplement that pledge, or at any rate to give the people there what they have been led to expect thev would get.

In support of 1 the position taken by the hon. member for >
Halton (Mr. Henderson), and to show that j the government in certain places are carry- ' ingi out their ante-election pledges, made by some of their speakers-I regret very much < that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Prefontaine) is not in his place- i I will read from the West Durham newspaper, the ' Canadian Statesman,' of January 8th, 1902, previous to the election of the then candidate and the present hon. member for West Durham (Mr. Beith), to 1 show that these gentlemen did make promises on that occasion and that they are now fulfilling them. On January 8th, 1902, the ' Canadian Statesman ' said :
Conservatives in this town know that Robert Beith can get government favours for this town if any man can, and that Mr. Thornton would be unable to accomplish anything. We want a new post office and customs house, don't we '! Other ridings have received new public buildings. "We want our share of patronage but can only get it by sending a government supporter to ask for it. Return Mr. Beith to parliament and Bowmanville will get these necessary public buildings.
I am glad to see that the Postmaster General (Hon. Sir Wm. Mulock) is carrying out the ante-electioni pledges of the Liberal party. In another instance this paper says :
For 18 years the Conservatives were in power at Ottawa. Millions of dollars were dispensed for public buildings and otherwise during that period, but not a dollar for West Durham till the Liberals got into power, then necessary grants were made to keep Newcastle and Bowmanville harbour piers from being washed into the lake. Millions of bushels of grain have been shipped from time to time from these | harbours for West Durham farmers and will still be in years to come. Further assistance is needed. Bowmanville badly needs a new post office and custom house and Robert Beith can get these also. Vote for him and see what he will do.
I am delighted to see that the hon. Postmaster General is carrying out the bribe-1 beg pardon-the pre-election pledge, as I had better put it, made to the electors of West Durham and Bowmanville. On December 25th, in the same paper, I find this :
There is also the matter of patronage and legislation in the interests of West Durham. Does any oue suppose for one moment that Mr. Thornton could get any favours Tor us from this government ? To imagine such a thing would be the height of absurdity. Few people know what Robert Beith has already done along these lines. At this very time the rubber factory is supplying goods to the government railways on orders secured through Mr. Beith's inQuence. Then we have got to have a new post office and custom house. There must no longer be any ifs or buts on this public necessity. This town needs a new post office and must have one very soon and Mr. Beith is the one man who can get it if any man can. We have waited patiently for better times, now we have the good times and Bowmanville wants a new building suited to the requirements of a post office and a custom
house. We believe that if Robert Beith is elected we shall get it-in short order too. We are not urging this as a reason altogether for supporting Mr. Beith,

'
Not altogether ; of course they had some other things.
But if we want a public building, we are not
as likely to get it if we send a man opposed to the government as if we sent one to support it.
I am delighted, when quoting these statements in support of the position taken by the hon. member for Halton, to see that the hon. Postmaster General and Minister of Labour is carrying out the pre-election bribe offered to the people of West Durham. The reason I have read these statements is that on an occasion, not very long since, the hon. member for West Durham positively denied that an appeal was made to the electors of West Durham along those lines. I have quoted from the Liberal paper statements made on the eve of the election there, and now the hon. gentlemen opposite are delivering the goods.

I may say to the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) that I will be pleased to call the attention of the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries to the subject that he has mentioned. However, he will have an opportunity when the estimates of that department come before the Committee to urge the importance of having a light at that point. I think something should be done in the matter. It occurred to me when the hon. member for Victoria (Sir. Hughes) i was speaking that he must have been supporting the hon. member for West Dur-1 ham (Mr. Beith), because the statements he quoted reminded me very much of his own ( writing in his spicy paper the Lindsay ' ' Warder.' However, my hon. friend must know that it is only on the merits of the ' ease that I have asked for this vote.

Postmaster General and to the hon. 5 Minister of Public Works, but especially to 3 the hon. Postmaster General when he goes 3 up around the methylated spirits mauu-" 1 factory where he gets good rake offs, and ~ I would suggest that we might have a com-j mittee or a commission at Ottawa as well e as ht Toronto.

S' This is for building a wharf at Burk's Falls. r There is an extension of the Grand Trunk g Railway which renders available thirty _ or a forty miles of navigation, and people bring

clown a great deal of material to be transshipped at that point. The Committee knows this is a newly settled part of the country, needing assistance. I think the money is well expended. The pier is under contract, the price being $5,400.
Is that the total cost 7

The total cost will be about $6,000.
Burlington channel piers-works of renewal and repair under contract, $50,000.

This work is under contract. The vote of $50,000 is required to make provision for completing the works, for the renewal and repairs under contract in connection with the reconstruction of the pier on the south side of Burlington channel. The total amount of the contract is $96,700.
May I ask the hon. minister if the work on the Burlington piers will be completed this summer 7

The expectation is that this work will be completed this summer. I have had representations made urging that it is necessary that this work should be completed, and instructions have been given to proceed with the work as quickly as possible. There has been some delay, but a great deal of material is on the ground and the work is proceeding very much more quickly than for some time past.

The work has been going on very slowly since the first appropriation was made, and if this appropriation is going to be expended on the same, principle we are not likely to finish it within the next ten years. I notice that on an expenditure of $1,500 over $700 has been spent for advertising. I do not think we can build piers very quickly under these conditions.
The report of the engineer just received says that the work is proceeding very much more expeditiously than it has been in the past.

I think it is proper to call the attention of the hon. Minister of Public Works to an item that appears in the expenditure of last year in reference to the estimate now asked for-Burlington channel, repairs to piers. The present item is to cover repairs to piers, and in the Auditor General's Report of 1902, page Y-263, we find $1,521.15 expended on repairs to piers of which $733.22 are for advertising. There seems to be too much advertising for the amount of work done there.
Depot Harbour-breakwater, $75,000.
How much was spent on that work last year 7
I must say that this work has not-proceeded

very rapidly. It was let at a season of the year when the class of timber which had to be ordered and cut in special sizes could not be obtained. However, I do not regret the delay because since looking into this work with the engineers, I believe we can make a change in the construction that will be much in the public interest and it is my intention to recommend that change. It will cost just about the same as the work under contract, but it will give greater accommodation to the public. The present contract is for a breakwater 1,700 feet long by twenty feet wide, and it is proposed to reduce the length of the breakwater to 500 feet, which will be sufficient to protect the present wharf but to make it very much wider so that two railway tracks can be laid down, and also afford a wharf for the accommodation of the general public. This is one of the very best harbours in the province. It is the only harbour I know of that requires very little work in the way of dredging after the piers are erected. A great deal of business is carried on there and it has been represented to me that a great deal of lumber is being brought down to this harbour to be shipped to different parts of Canada and also for export to the New England States especially. I believe that without increasing the amount of the estimate we can provide a great deal better accommodation for the public.
What was the amount of the contract for the present work 7
It was let by contract for $195,000.
How much has already been spent 7
Was it let to the lowest tenderer 7
Yes. I may say that my intention is to recommend the continuation of the present contract; it is doubling up the work instead of continuing it out as I have explained.
What explanation does the minister give os to the changes he proposes to inqke 7

The present contract provides for a pier 1,700 feet long and twenty feet wide. I find that the pier can be shortened so as to give sufficient protection, and widened to eighty feet, on which we can put two tracks of railways. The water is deep and boats can unload on both sides of the wharf. When a boat arrives with lumber it is very desirable to have accommodation to land that lumber, because you cannot always land it from the boat into the railway car. We hope that the trade of that port will grow so that perhaps in the future the wharf and

pier may have to be extended, but at all events we are dealing with the present now.
Was not the contract let to Mr. Davis.
The contractors are Davis, Haney and Millar.
Was the contract not let for $157,500 ?
The contract for the crib work is for $157,500, but there is $37,500 for rip-rap.
What revenue will the government derive from this wharf which is going to cost $200,000 ?

It is impossible to tell exactly what the direct revenue will be, but every one who has studied the development of that district will know that the indirect benefit to all Canada will be very great. Something like 15,000,000 bushels of wheat were shipped through Depot Harbour last year, and this will give increased facilities for shipping not only grain but lumber and other commodities as well.

How does the minister propose to adjust the account, because his contemplated changes will apparently alter the nature of the whole work. Who makes an estimate of what the difference in the cost will be ?

There is no change made at present but I thought it my duty to tell the House that I had those changes in contemplation. The estimates are made by the chief engineer of the department. It is not so difficult to get at the details after all, and before the work is proceeded with I shall submit to the House the plans proposed by the chief engineer.

The suspicious thing about it is this : That the departmental engineer gets out a plan for a certain work, recommends that as suitable for the locality, a contract is let for a large sum of money, $10,000 is spent and then the engineer changes the whole plan. It would indicate that the first plan was made on poor judgment and imperfect knowledge, or otherwise there would not be any necessity for changing it so very soon. The next question is how to make even an approximate estimate of the difference in the value of the work now as compared with the original contract. There is always an amount of suspicion attached to a transaction where a radical change is made in a work shortly after a contract is let, and an arrangement is made privately between the minister and the contractor as to what shall be paid for the work. The practice, I think, is very bad. It might be, if the minister invited tenders for the work he proposes to do now,
that he would receive tenders for doing it at a very much lower figure than it is likely to cost. At any rate, the public have had no opportunity of tendering for this new work.

My hon. friend is altogether mistaken. It is quite true, perhaps, the minister might have made this change without consulting parliament, but I am not in favour of doing business in that way. I thought it my duty in making the change, to submit the recommendation to parliament. Neither is it correct to say that the chief engineer exercised bad judgment under the existing conditions when he recommended this pier to be built as it is. I am the one responsible for looking into the work, advising the recommendation, and asking parliament to endorse my recommendation. If there was anything suspicious about it I would be very sorry to be accused of anything of the kind, and I certainly would not submit a proposition to make a change which I did not think warranted in the public interest and likely to receive the endorsement of the members of this House. My view of the matter at any rate is that a great deal more public benefit can be got for the expenditure by the changed plan. As to calculating the price, my hon. friend will know that for the same class of work there are so many cubic feet to be done under contract, and by the change there will be no advantage to the contractor and no disadvantage to the public.

The minister says the work can be estimated, but in one instance you have two face walls, 1,700 feet long with 25 feet between them and in the other two face walls 500 feet long with 80 feet between them, and you must fill in between them. That kind of work can be done very much more cheaply where there is a wide space between the walls than where there is a narrow space.

My hon. friend will see that there are so many cubic feet of timber work, stone work, or earth work, as the case may be. We are not going to pay any more than will be paid for the same class of work under contract. However, I am not asking for any change, but I have taken the first opportunity to intimate to the House what I thought would be in the public interest. If, when I submit the proposition and the plans to the House, it does not receive the endorsement of the House, I will carry the work out as it is. But I feel so confident that it will receive the unanimous endorsement of the House that I propose to make the recommendation.
Will this work when completed belong to the government ?

Yes, this is a government work.

Of course, I do not object to the expenditure of the money, but it appeared to me that a breakwater was quite a different thing from a wharf. I have always understood that a breakwater was built for the protection of a harbour. I think that is in the public interest; but I do not think it right that the government should build a wharf from which they will receive no revenue, simply for the benefit of some corporation. I think that is an important harbour, and that it is in the public interest that it should be improved; but I do not think it necessary to double up the breakwater and provide space for railway tracks for the benefit of some individual corporation to make money out of at the expense of the public. That is the way it strikes me.

I may say to my hon. friend that the very opposite is the case, and I know that I shall have his endorsement. This is not for the benefit of any corporation. A breakwater is often used as a landing pier, and there is no reason why it should not be, and by making this change we shall get a very much needed wharf which will be of great advantage to the public. I am sure that when I bring down the plans the hon. gentleman will agree with me.

The hon. minister says that when we see the plans we shall be perfectly satisfied; but the very few moments that 'we have to look at plans which are laid on the Table at the very time the item is voted, afford little opportunity to obtain any information, or to exercise a judgment on the matter in hand. I am not saying that this work is wrong; it may be all right; I am only objecting to the principle of making radical changes in an important work like this after the contract is let. I still contend that the party who does the work could do it very much cheaper by filling up a space of 80 feet wide than by filling up a space of 25 feet wide, because In the larger space we could use almost any kind of material. Then, letting a contract for a certain kind of work, and telling the House that is what is needed, and the House accepting that information as correct and voting the money on the strength of it. and the next year coming back and practically changing the whole plan, at least arouses a suspicion in our minds that the matter could not have been well considered in the first instance, or that there must be some special reason for making so radical a change, and we want to know what it is. Then, the other question comes up which we have often debated in this House, of changing large contracts on the recommendation of the engineer and putting it into the hands of the contractor and the government to manipulate the figures between themselves as to what shall be paid for the work.

I will bring down the plan and lay it on Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
the Table, so that my hon. friend will have an opportunity of examining it before I make any recommendation.
Did the government build Depot Harbour ?

There has been a lot of work done by the Canada Atlantic Railway at Depot Harbour in the way of wharfs and elevators for its own purposes, but this is for the shipping interests, and I do not know of any work the government has undertaken which is so much in the public interest as Depot Harbour.
I understand that Mr. Booth has spent about $750,000 on this Depot Harbour.
That would be on wharfs and elevators in connection with his own work, but not in connection with this.

If this is a breakwater protecting the harbour, what part of this harbour does the government own ? Does the government own it all or does the Canada Atlantic Railway or Mr. Booth own any part of this harbour which the government is now protecting ?
This work is for the benefit of the harbour and for the advantages of shippers outside the railway and is under the complete control of the government.
Therefore the interests of Mr. Booth and those of the government will not conflict in any way ?
Not at all.
Will the hon. minister bring down the tenders received for that work ?
Yes.
Is the work going on now ?

The contract is let, the timber has all been got out, and the change can be made at present without loss to the country. I will bring down the plan and submit the change I propose to the House, and if the House does not approve, no change will be made.
I do not desire to dispute the statement of the hon. minister, but would it not be a more business-like proposition to bring down the amended plan before asking us to pass the item ?

The House is already committed to the contract. It is a legal, binding contract, and the only question is whether the change I propose would commend itself to the good sense of the House. If not, we will go on with the work as originally contemplated.

It seems to me that this is rather an unusual proceeding, but I am going to accept the statement of the hon. minister, and he says we will get full information when the plan is brought down.
Georgian Bay, Point au Baril route-improvement of the Devil's Elbow channel between Parry Sound and Killarney, $3,000.
What improvements are you making there ?
This is a vote to provide for the improvement of the channel. It is being pressed by the navigators and is very necessary, it is for the removal of a shoal that is very dangerous to shipping.
That is by dredging ?
Xes, and blasting too.
Are you doing it with your own dredge or by contract and day's work.
We have no dredge there to do the work and will have to make arrangements for a dredge at the usual terms.
What are the terms ?
It depends altogether on the size of the dredge and its capacity for work-$8 to $12 per hour, if by the hour, and if by contract, so much per yard.
What do you pay per yard ?
The average price would be about thirteen cents.
How do you do the blasting work ?

Under the supervision of our own engineer and not by contract. It is very difficult in a small work like this in a channel to make any specifications. It would take the appropriation to make them.
Goderich harbour works, $16,000.
This is for renewing the original portion of the old superstructure of the pier. The total cost of repairing is $16,000.

How is the work to be
done ?

It would be somewhat difficult for me to pledge myself without further information, as to whether this would be done more advantageously under the supervision of an engineer and by hiring labour, than by letting a contract. If specifications can be prepared, I prefer to let a contract, but if not we will have to hire our own labour and buy material.
Does this constitute all that the people of Goderich demand from the Department of Public Works ?

No, demands have been made, not only from Goderich, but the whole of the district and from Toronto West, that a breakwater should be built at that port. I myself believe it is a matter of necessity, if we are to have the benefit we should have on Lake Huron. At present mostly all the shipping goes up the American side of the lake because we have not any harbour of refuge on the Canadian side. There are in addition splendid facilities already erected there in the shape of an elevator and other improvements at the harbour. I am very muoh impressed with the representation that a great deal of the grain of the west might be taken caye of here if we had the proper facilities. However, the discussion of that matter will come up more properly when I ask the House to consider an appropriation for the purpose of improving Goderich harbour.
I do not think it is a local work, but national in its nature, and the shipments to Canadian ports depend a great deal on our being able to take care of the grain which comes to these lake ports. Larger vessels could come to Goderich than to many of the other places. I am informed by the Grand Trunk that they would be prepared to take care of the grain and that perhaps from fifteen to twenty millions of bushels could be easily handled if there was a very moderate expenditure on the harbour.
Goderich is not a harbour of refuge in any sense at the present time.

For want of protection to the boats coming in, it is almost impossible, I am informed, to take a vessel into the harbour. I am informed by lake captains that if, following the experience of some of the ports on the American side, a pier were built out to break the rolling of the sea, a vessel might enter the harbour with some safety, and they could use it as well as they do the harbours on the other side of the line.
Would the breakwater be an expensive undertaking ?

I think not. I intended to look into the matter more fully and have a further report from the engineers as to the character and cost of the work. I think that at least a test might be made at very moderate expense. Representations have been made to me that the cost of a breakwater such as would make this a first class harbour of refuge is in the neighbourhood of a couple of hundred thousand dollars.

I have many communications from 'that part of the country with regard to the harbour, and they say that for two hundred miles along the shore of Lake Huron there is not a safe harbour

for steamers to enter in case of storm. The grain men and millers all through that part of the country are very anxious to have the harbour put into proper shape. I may say also that I have a resolution passed by the Board of Trade of Stratford, and letters and telegrams from Mitchell, Seaforth, Goderich and all along that line; and I think the government should do something to put the harbour into proper shape. So far as I am concerned, I will do everything in my power to help them.
Is this $16,000 to be spent on the two jetties that run out there, or on some work in the bay ?
It is to be spent on the pier on the south side of the entrance channel.

Speaking about the contemplated expenditure for the purpose of a breakwater, I understand that the hon. gentleman does not consider that to be a work specially for the benefit of the harbour of Goderich, but one of national importance that must be undertaken by the government-to provide a harbour of refuge and put the harbour into such shape that large grain carriers can come in.
Who owns the dock inside ?
It is government property.
Is the elevator on the government pier ?
I am sorry to say that I am not sufficiently familiar with the locality to be able to say whether the elevator is on that pier or not. I do not think it is.

With the permission of the Committee, I will read a brief extract from the letter of the mayor of Goderich :
Buffalo handled 12,000,000 bushels of Canadian grain in 1902. Goderich has an elevator capacity of slightly over 20,000,000 bushels a season, but we handled only three millions and a-half bushels last year because our harbour cannot be entered in the fall after bad weather.
That gives an idea of the business that might be done.

The mayor of Goderich, over his own signature stated that $730,328.70 had been spent on the Goderich harbour. Can the minister inform us in what way this' was spent ? Was it in dredging, in breakwaters, or how ?

The amount given by the department; is $713,341.43, much the same as the amount stated by the mayor. This covers the expenditure from 1850. The money was spent in dredging, building wharfs, making repairs, &c.
There was a breakwater there at one time, has it gone to pieces ?

I think the present pier was swept away, but it was rebuilt. It is not the protection we are speaking of-which, of course, has nothing to do with this vote, but the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Kemp) brought it to the attention of the Committee.

But what I am asking about is the breakwater which was once there-a very good work. There was a good deal of shipping in Goderich harbour at one time. It seems to me that the difficulty with regard to Goderich harbour and the Maitland river is that when the ice thaws in the spring and the water comes down, the sand is carried out between the piers and prevents vessels coming in. It seems to me if they had a cut and a breakwater such as they had before, it would put the harbour into such shape that shipping could come in as before.
Is there any revenue from this dock ?
I cannot answer my hon. friend. As he knows, that is another department, and would come under another head.

I notice that, according to the report:
The timbers are in a very much decayed condition, in some instances it being difficult to find sufficient sound old timber to spike the new timber to, and these remarks will hold good with reference to the south pier as well. Some slight repairs should he made to both north and south piers as well as to the check-water. . . . These repairs will be only temporary, as the timbers of both piers are so badly decayed their superstructure should be completely renewed within two or three years, or breeches will be washed through into the newly dredged channel.
Evidently, the works are not in very good condition. I noticed in the letter advocating this being made a harbour of refuge, which, I suppose every member got, it is stated that we have spent a very large amount of money already. Perhaps as much as three-quarters of a million in that harbour and that if we did not spend more the work would be of no use. But this would suggest either that the expenditure has not been wisely carried on or that the harbour is a very difficult one to make. And, if we make further heavy expenditure, we may find we are still without the harbour of refuge. As to making the harbour fit for grain carriers to come in, I think that should be done, but whether we should spend so much in making a harbour of refuge is another question. On the basis of the information we have, it seems a very doubtful question whether it would be well to do that.

That is hardly under consideration now. At

the same time, I may say, I am having further information collected with regard to the question, I have consulted some of the captains of the vessels in those waters, who, after all, are the practical men. They gave their experience with regard to similar works erected in places on the American shore. They know something of the advantages of breakwaters such as is proposed for Goderich. Of course, conditions vary in different places. It may be to some extent an experiment, but I think that, from the experience on the American shore we should be perfectly safe in making the improvement I speak of. It would not require a very extravagant expenditure to make the trial. As to what effect the breakwater would have in making this a harbour of refuge, I have asked the engineer to prepare a plan of the shortest breakwater that could be built there that would have the desired effect of allowing ships to enter the harbour. In that way-of course, I may be mistaken; it was an idea of my own-I think it possible that we might, for a very reasonable expenditure, learn what the effect of the larger one would be at that point.
Are you proposing to repair all these docks ? What interest have we, for instance, in the Grand Trunk dock ? I see that is very much out of repair, and is a menace to both life and navigation.

I have no doubt the Grand Trunk Railway will repair their own dock. I may say that they joined a deputation in making representations to the minister in favour of an appropriation. But none of this vote is to be spent dn the property of the Grand Trunk Railway, or on any other property. It is for the improvement of government piers.
Is it not possible to have specifications prepared and tenders called for this work ?
I am not prepared to pledge myself, but I may say that I prefer to let this work by contract if the specifications can be prepared.

I can understand how the Grand Trunk Railway would desire to press upon the government the expenditure of a large sum of money ; but I think private docks should be kept *up by private corporations.
Harbours, rivers and bridges-general repairs and improvements to $15,000.
Where does the hon. gentleman propose to spend the largest part of this item ?

I find that last year $15,000 were spent at Beaverton, Burk's Falls, Goderich, Huntsville, Hawkestone, Marksville, North Bay, Port Findlay, etc. For the current year-small sums were expended at Bruce Mines,
Kingston graving dock, Lancaster, North Bay, Presqu'ile, Summerston and Sydenham river, &c.; and generally a sum of $7,000 for different works throughout the province.
Is some of this money to be expended in repairing the dock at Presqu'ile ?
Does that property belong to the government or to a private corporation ?
I have not the information. I was reading out the items that were spent.

I would like to know why the Minister of Public Works should expend money on that work. It does not belong to the government, it is owned by a private party. It seems strange that the government should spend money there on a work from which they receive no revenue whatever.

If the principle is to expend this money on private docks as well as on government docks, we want to know it. Some of us have private docks in our constituencies, and we might approach the hon. gentleman with the view of getting some money expended on them.

At a previous sitting of the House I said that I was surprised to find that so much money had been spent in previous years on this class of works. I am rather surprised that the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Ingram) should have supported for so many years a government in voting money to be expended on private docks. I am not prepared to say at the present moment that there might not be a justification, in the public interest, in spending money on a wharf which, though not owned by the government, might be used by the public at a nominal charge. But generally speaking, I think it would be much better that properties on which public money is spent should be vested in the Crown. It is also true that through municipal assistance private companies have built works on the lake shore and at other points, and it seems that the government has been aiding them on the ground that they were of public utility.

My experience with the Conservative party has not been such as the hon. gentleman intimates. A number of years ago I asked for a small amount of money for Port Stanley harbour. It was owned by the London and Port Stanley Railway, the Grand Trunk Railway Company had it leased, and the government refused to spend any money on that harbour until it was transferred to the government, and after it was transferred to the government, then I was able to obtain a small amount for that harbour.
What evidence has the hon. gentleman that that harbour was transferred to the government ?

I myself held the documents some years ago relating to the transfer. But my principal reason for rising was to remind the hon. gentleman that in my constituency there is a harbour which is contributing towards licenses. Their money is being paid into the hands of the government, and while the government is willing to receive money from the fishermen at that port, they are unwilling to expend any towards fixing up the harbour for the benefit of the fishermen. The fact that by a recent judicial decision the license fees from the fishermen are now handed over to the Ontario government should be no reason why these men should be deprived by this government of the enjoyment of a proper harbour.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Is any part of this $15,000 to be expended in the harbour at Gananoque ? When the late Minister of Public Works visited that town I think he promised the deputation who waited on him that something would be done. While speaking on this point I would ask the hon. minister if he would kindly have an engineer from his department go up there and see the work that is going on now. The Rathbun Company are rebuilding a dock over 300 feet long. It was originally built with timber and filled with stone. They have taken the timber down below the water line and they are renewing the whole work with concrete. It will cost a very large sum of money but when they get the dock completed they will not have sufficient water outside to allow vessels of deep draft to approach laden with coal. I presume there are more arrivals, as you will notice by the report of the customs department, at Gananoque than at any other port on the Canadian side of the lake. I think the least the government can do is to make a fair appropriation for the necessary dredging before public docks. Not a dollar has ever been spent by the government on the dock at Gananoque; indeed, all the docks have been built by private parties, but unfortunately we have not a sufficient depth of water. I think it would be in the interest of the country generally if, in place of renewing docks and piers with timber as the government are doing, they should commence doing as all towns are doing, that is, putting down permanent sidewalks, doing away with the wood and putting in concrete. I think it would be well if the hon. minister would send one of his men to inspect the work that is now nearing completion at Gananoque.
The matter mentioned by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) has been brought to

mj attention and it is under consideration to make provision for dredging at the point he has mentioned as well as at Kingston. We have to realize that the larger boats now in use make deeper dredging necessarv. I have asked for an increase of $5,000 in that province for this general work of dredging. Considering the size of the province and the number of harbours that have to be dredged it is a very small amount and I think that after the estimate is made up we may have to ask for probably an increase of $5,000, because, I believe, a great deal of satisfactory work can be done by the government dredges if we had sufficient money to do a lot of work that we now let by contract. It costs so much to move these private dredges from place to place while if there is a bar filling up, such as the hon. member for South Leeds refers to at Gananoque, the government dredge can be sent without any extra expense being incurred because the employees are under pay, and good effective work can be done at these various harbours. I agree with the hon. gentleman as to the advantage of concrete over wooden work, especially now that we cannot get the class of timber that was formerly available. I have been pressing on the engineer's department my own personal view in regard to this matter and the superstructures of many of the new works we are undertaking, or rather the works that parliament is committed to and which were only commenced since I took office, are being made of concrete. With modern machinery and the improved method of making concrete you can build a concrete work of a considerable size for the same price as a first-class timber work and it will wear a great deal longer.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The Rathbun's who are large lumber dealers claim that they can put in a concrete wharf cheaper than a timber one. The large steamers owned by the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Company and plying between Toronto and Kingston refused to call at Gananoque because of the insufficient depth of water.

I am surprised to hear the statement of the hon. Minister of Public Works that they had not money enough to keep the dredges going. I always thought the contention was that the government had not dredges enough to do the work. Parliament has never been niggardly in voting all the money required to keep the government dredges going. We have always heard the complaint that we could not use up the money by employing government dredges and that we had to hire private dredges.

We have not had dredges at points where there has been considerable work to do. At some places the dredging has been in deeper water than the dredges we had in Canada are able to work. There are many such places not only in Ontario but especially in the lower provinces. I find that we have an-

other vote for general dredging out of which I propose to have this work done at different points, where it is required.

You do not intend to have dredging done to any great depth at Gananoque. I presume you could not dredge very deeply there because otherwise you would undermine the concrete wall, so that there could not be any very deep dredging there. I did not know there was on the Georgian Bay very much deep dredging required to be done.
No, I was speaking generally.
I want to ask the hon. minister if he can give us any idea of the number of private wharfs upon which we are spending government money and the number of wharfs belonging to the country.
I will be very pleased to have a statement prepared.
And where they are ?
Yes, where they are located and the number. There is quite a number.

I know there is and I always thought the principle a bad one. I can understand that in the early history of the country where private enterprise would construct a dock that was valuable to the country it might be justified, but I never could understand the wisdom of spending large sums of money on building up private property, the revenue of which went entirely to the individual. There are examples of this at Sault Ste. Marie and Bruce Mines. I see you have a dock at Hawkestone in the county of Simcoe. The government can have no interest in that.
A boat called there last summer.

Was there one ? Well, that is a revelation. I was not aware that any but row boats called there. I hold that the principle is wrong. Where private individuals reap the rewards of our expenditure and the country receives practically no benefit from it beyond the convenience of shipping over the dock, it does seem to me that we are not justified in carrying this practice to the length we have done for many years. Two years ago, I understand, it was proposed to buy that Presqu' isle wharf. Now, I am told that that dock has not been in use for years and years and it is of no value to the public. The government made some kind of a preliminary contract to buy this dock which was of no use to the public, and the purchase of which would be beneficial to no one except the estate which owned the property.

The minister has stated that the practice has prevailed for a great many years of expending public money on
private docks, and he asks for money tonight to continue that policy. He has promised the hon. member for Grey (Mr. Sproule) that he will bring down a statement showing the number of private properties on which public money has been expended. I would ask the minister what is his own opinion in respect to this policy ? Does he intend to continue to ask the House for votes of this kind in the future ?

These small votes are in order to complete works already under way. I may say to my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) that I am not in favour of the policy. So much is that the case that I asked the other night for a vote to purchase a wharf instead of spending money in improving private property, but hon. gentlemen opposite, acting within their right, thought that I should not be trusted to take over that property until they got further information. Generally speaking, I am not in favour of this policy, and I do not think I shall come down with a new vote asking for such an expenditure unless I am able to give special reasons that will commend themselves to parliament. I am pleased that the hon. gentleman made the suggestion that we should have a list of such works owned by private parties or corporations; so that we will see what reason, if any, there is for continuing the expenditure of public money on such works. I find that the owners put a very high estimate upon some of these works, and there is a conflict between the government and the private owners as to their value. Generally speaking, I am in favour of spending public money only on the property of the Crown.

I notice that the Minister of Customs and the Minister of Marine are absent, and I again am compelled to lodge a complaint against these ministers for their lack of attention to the public business. I want to submit a question to the Minister of Public Works which I presume could be better answered by the Minister of Customs, with reference to the transaction of public business on these private wharfs. What I desire to know is : How does the government protect the revenue of the country against the importation of goods through harbours and docks of this character, as I understand that there are no wharfingers or public officers in charge of them ?

I think the answer to that is simple. You ship subject to duty or in bond, and notice is sent to the customs officers, and if any parties are trying to smuggle they would be detected on a private wharf just as well as on a public wharf or anywhere else.

We voted at the last sitting $9,000 for the Blind river wharf. Was that property purchased by the Crown, and if so at what price ?

The MINISTER OB' PUBLIC WORKS. The property was purchased at $400, speaking from memory.
Last year the Minister, of Public Works told us that the price fixed for the property was $250. How did it come to increase ?
That was probably the estimated cost, but the price was $400 about.

I wish to make a brief statement in respect to some money that was proposed to be expended on'Port Credit harbour in the county of Peel, and which harbour is owned by private individuals. Some years ago this matter was brought to the attention of the government and there was considerable correspondence with the council of the township in which that harbour is situated. The township council was told distinctly that the policy of the government was that they did not expend any public money upon harbours owned by private individuals. It seems surprising, in view of that statement, that at that time and up to the present large amounts of money are being expended by the government on harbours owned by private individuals. I direct the attention of the minister to the fact that Port Credit harbour is a very important harbour for that section of the country, and the expenditure of money there would be in the interest of the public generally. Last winter the cost of coal was a very important consideration to the farmers, and it would be in the interest of the people there if money were expended on these harbours upon that part of Lake Ontario, so that the people would have the opportunity of competing in coal by reason of the fact that coal laden vessels could come there. The pier of that harbour is in a very bad condition, and the harbour requires dredging.
Is that harbour under municipal or private ownership ?

It is partly private and partly municipal ownership. I am surprised that the government should continue the policy of expending money on private harbours in face of the statement made to the township council to which I have referred. Perhaps I could get the minister to say that out of this vote of $15,000 which is to be expended on harbours partly owned by the government and partly by private individuals, that he would send his engineer up to look over Port Credit harbour, and to report to him if something could not be done.

As I said, I am personally opposed to spending money on private harbours. In this case, municipal ownership makes the work somewhat in the public interest, and I shall be pleased to grant the request of the hon.

gentleman and have a report made upon it, and see how it stands.
Lake Temiscamingue-wharfs, $5,500.
Is this a new wharf ?

This is for two wharfs for the accommodation of tlje people of that district. One will cost about $9,000 and the other about $1,500.
Midland harbour-dredging, $12,000.
Where is Midland harbour ?
My hon. friend must know that Midland is going to be the Buffalo of Canada. It is one of the most important harbours of Ontario.
I notice that a vessel was agrouM there the other day. What is the depth of water ?
It varies from fifteen to twenty-one feet. It is the intention to make a channel a uniform depth of twenty-one feet.

I would like to ask the minister if the warehouses and the dock, for which the town paid $10,000, have been deeded to the government, have they been rented, who has rented the dock and who the warehouse, and what rental is paid ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC W'ORKS. These matters have not been attended to yet. We only got the deeds a short time ago, and this week is the first opportunity I have had of asking the chief engineer of the department and one of the principal officials to visit the harbour. As soon as I receive the report I shall be able to give information on this and other matters.

I may say that there is one large warehouse and two smaller ones, and also an excellent dock at which boats now land. All these being now the property of the Dominion, I think it would be in the public interest and in the interest of fair play that the department should ask for public tenders for the use of them, and that they should not be given to any person without competition. May I ask the minister if he promises that that will be done ?
Yes, that will be attended to.

I may say that they have been rented, I understand, for $500 a year, which I think is a small rent.
Oakville-repairs to pier, &c., $6,000.
Will this vote put this dock in a thorough state of repair ?

The report of the engineer shows details indicating that this will complete the work and put it in good shape.

000.	Now with regard to reduction of public debt, it may be well to notice that it is very seldom the lot of a Finance Minister of Canada to be able to speak of a reduction of the public debt. Some hon. gentlemen, who may not have followed this matter closely, may be surprised to learn that prior to the advent of this government, only twice in the history of the Dominion of Canada was there a reduction of the public debt. Once in our time, prior to the present, have we had a reduction of the public debt, amounting to upwards of $700,000, and now, in the present year, we have this large reduction to which I have referred. While presenting these figures, let me frankly say that I do not think any Minister of Finance of this country should be expected to show often a reduction of the public debt. In a new country like Canada with a great many public works requiring to be assisted, with many demands on the treasury, it would not be surprising that each year we would not only be obliged to spend our ordinary revenue but to incur some debt in order to carry on our great public works.
That, Sir, has been the experience of Canada during the greater part of its history. Where we have had surpluses-and we have had many of them-almost invariably they have been absorbed by the expenditures on capital account. Only four times in the history of Canada have there been reductions in the public debt. That is to say, there have been only four years in which the Dominion was able to provide for all its expenditures and have a balance wherewith to reduce the debt. Not only was the subject discussed again and again in the conference, but we had frequent opportunities of discussing it with the British ministers individually, and particularly with Mr. Chamberlain and Mr. Gerald Balfour, the president of the Board of Trade. We contended, as appears in the blue-book containing the proceedings of the conference, that the preference was not only of sentimental value but also of great material value to the British trader and manufacturer. While we contended that the preference already granted was of more value to Great Britain than the British officials had I been disposed to admit, we told them that ! if the imperial government were prepared ! to adopt the preferential policy and give our 1 products exemption from the duties now imposed or hereafter to be imposed on foreign goods, we would be prepared to grant some furtiier preference, subject to certain .conditions which were clearly laid down. We frankly stated that we could not undertake to give that further preference in a manner which would operate to the disadvantage of our own industries. As between the British manufacturer and the- Canadian manufacturer, we thought we had gone as far in the way of reduction of duties as we could. But we pointed out that Canada consumed a large quantity of goods imported from foreign countries; and in return for the preference which we sought for Canada, we were prepared to so rearrange our tariff as to give Great Britain a further preference, not over the Canadian manufacturer, but over the foreign competitor.

The general resolution that was finally adopted as covering the principle underlying the several proposals comprised in Mr. Balfour's memorandum, was as follows :-*
1.	That this conference recognizes that the principle of preferential trade between the United Kingdom and His Majesty's dominions beyond the seas would stimulate and facilitate mutual commercial intercourse, and would by promoting the development ot the resources and industries of the several parts, strengthen the empire.
2.	That this conference recognizes that, in the present circumstances of the colonies, it is not practicable to adopt a general system of free trade as between the mother country and the British dominions beyond the seas.
3.	That with a view, however, to promoting the increase of trade within the empire, it is desirable that those colonies which have not already adopted such a policy should, as far as their circumstances permit, give' substantial preferential treatment to the products and manufactures of the United Kingdom.

This subject has frequently engaged the attention of the conference. At an early stage Mr. Chamberlain suggested that the question could most conveniently be considered by the representatives of each colony placing themselves in communication with the President of the Board of Trade, Mr. Gerald Balfour, and the officials of that department. Accordingly the Canadian ministers had several protracted interviews with these gentlemen, and discussed the whole subject very fully. Opportunity was also taken to present the Canadian view to Mr. Chamberlain. Now that the conference is drawing to a close, it is desirable that the course of the discussion, and the conclusions reached by the Canadian ministers, should be outlined and placed on record.
From the beginning of the proceedings the Canadian ministers have claimed that in consideration of the substantial preference given by Canada for some years to the products of the mother country, Canadian food products should be exempted in the United Kingdom from the duties recently imposed. Representations to this effect previously made through the High Commissioner for Canada were supplemented by the ministers, both in writing and in the personal interview's with the imperial ministers.
Mr. Chamberlain, on behalf of the imperial government, was unable to agree to the proposals of the Canadian ministers. He represented that the imperial government, while highly appreciating the good feefing manifested by Canada in the granting of preferential treatment, did not think the material results to the trade of the United Kingdom were as great as the Canadiarf ministers claimed. He further said that the change desired by Canada would he an important departure from the 1 established fiscal policy of the Kingdom, and that if the proposals could be entertained at all, as to which he was not prepared to commit himself, it would he necessary for Canada to offer some material tariff concessions bevond those which she had already voluntarily given.
The Canadian ministers, therefore, submitted a memorandum on the subject of the advantages already received by Great Britain from the Canadian preferential tariff, with a view to showing that these were of much value, and entitled to weight in the consideration of the whole subject.	>

If, after using every effort to bring about such a readjustment of the fiscal policy of the empire, the Canadian government should find that the principle of preferential trade is not acceptable to the colonies generally, or the mother country, then Canada should be free to take such action as might be deemed necessary in the presence of such conditions.

Surprise lias been expressed in some quarters-I have heard it expressed, I think, in this House-that the colonial conference did not produce some more definite result. ^ I think that that is the result of some misapprehension. Tire colonial conference was not a legislative body; it was not what could be called an executive body; it was at the best merely an advisory body. All it could do was to consider the various subjects brought before it, and to express the conclusions which might be reached by the gentlemen comprising it, leaving to all the governments concerned the duty of taking up the matter later on if it should be deemed necessary. That is exactly the position in "which this matter of preferential trade stands to-day. The end is not yet. We are not prepared to say at this moment what may be the answer of the British government with regard to the view we have placed before it.
We are aware, Sir, that Mr. Chamberlain, the able Colonial Secretary,, whose interest and support we would naturally desire and hope to obtain, has been for some months absent in South Africa, where he has rendered very valuable service to the empire. While we are glad that he was there to render that service in the pacification of South Africa, his absence has(>
perhaps, to some extent, been a loss to us, inasmuch as, had he been in London during these six months, we might have had his valuable help in the consideration of this matter. The budget speech of the new Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Ritchie, has not_ yet been delivered. We are so close to it, that it may be too much to expect that this subject would be dealt with in it. But, however that may be, this much at least may be said-that, as we were invited by Mr. Chamberlain to express our views on this subject, as he took an interest in the matter, and as there are others in the imperial parliament who take an interest in it, some of whom are prepared to express themselves more freely than Mr. Chamberlain himself was prepared to do, the least that the British authorities can expect is that we shall [DOT]allow a reasonable time to elapse before anything further is done. But if, after further consideration, they come to the conclusion that our request is not a reasonable one, if, owing to their adherence to certain views they cannot grant us the preference, we shall be free to take our own course. Whether, in such a case it! would be wise, in the interests of Canada, to modify or change the preferential tariff, would be a question to be considered. But, putting aside other considerations, if the British government and people do not show any appreciation of the value of the preference, then, so far as the British government and people are concerned, they cannot complain if we see fit to modify or change that preferential tariff. Of course, Sir, theie would still remain the more important consideration, how far, if at all, that tariff could be changed with due regard to the interest of the masses of the Canadian people.
Next to Great Britain, the country with which, in the past, we have been accustomed to say wre desire to deal, is the United States. I suppose it is not too much to say that, for some years, our friends across the border have not been too well disposed towards the admission of Canadian products into their markets. 'While from one point of view, we have been disposed j:o regret their attitude, there are other considerations which would dispose us to modify veiy much any expressions of dissatisfaction. When the people of Canada discovered, after frequent efforts, and after ample time given for consideration, that there was a stioi g hostility on the part of the United States authorities to granting liberal	arrangements, they ceased to grumble about the matter but, like sensible people, made up
