speakername: The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS (Hon. James Sutherland).

speechtext:
Would the Minister of Public Works please furnish the statement

which he promised to give us showing the blocks owned by private individuals on which we are spending public money ?

We have not been able to have that statement prepared yet. There is a good deal *of labour connected with it. There is no list in this form in the department, and all the items have to be gone over and the facts looked up. I hope to lay the statement on the Table to-morrow.
Port Hope-repairs to pier and dredging, $7,500.
It was stated that the amount appropriated last year would complete this work, but I see we are now asked this large sum in addition.

This is for the renewal of the superstructure of the east pier, for a length of one hundred feet by thirty-four feet and six feet high. I imagine that when they came to do the work, they found the pier in much worse *condition than had been anticipated. It is an old pier.
Is this a private dock or a government dock ?
A government dock.
Is the work being done by day labour, or by contract ?
By day labour.
Will this complete the work ?

Yes.
RiviSre aux Puces-repairs to pilework, $1,S00.
The minister has had this money for two years. How is it that no work was done last year ?

1 have received a petition lately showing that this is a very necessary work. It is to renew 200 feet of piling work on the west side and 130 feet on the east side. The total estimate is $1,800, so that this will *complete the work.
Where is this work ?
In Essex county.
There is no dredging ?

No, only piling.
River Ottawa-improvement of narrows at Petewawa, above Pembroke, $4,000.
Is this part of the Ottawa and Georgian Bay canal ?
I suppose it is.
This appears to be a revote. When was the appropriation first made ?

Some work seems to have been undertaken there some years ago. There is a rocky shoal which obstructs the steamboat channel through the narrows above Pembroke, and this money is to be expended in making a channel 100 feet wide, with a depth of eight feet at low water. I have not the information at hand to show when the appropriation was first made. But this is a very necessary work, as this shoal is an obstruction to navigation.
Has there been a considerable amount of money spent up to the present time on this work ?
Three thousand dollars.
Why was not this money spent last year ?
I am not able to give my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) that information. The information furnished to the department is that about 4,000 feet of this rocky shoal has to be removed.
How long has it been under contract '1
I cannot say.

I consider that the principle of these revotes is a very bad one. It is not right to apply for an appropriation in advance, before there is any definite scheme proposed, or any contemplation of an immediate expenditure. We cannot close our eyes to the fact that appropriations of this kind are, in some instances and by some governments, held dangling before the eyes of the electors for the purpose of influencing votes. I think I may say that in some cases that has been done by the present government. I protest against the principle as a bad one.
There might be such instances, but this is not one of them. It does not affect any constituency or any vote.
I can tell the hon. gentleman that there are some.
There may be. But this is for the purpose of removing a rocky shoal in the Ottawa river, for the benefit of boats that ply north of Pembroke.

When I say that appropriations are frequently put in the estimates for the purpose of influencing votes, I do not mean to say that the present one may be wholly improper. No doubt it is intended to kill two1 birds with one stone. It may

be intended both to serve a public purpose and to influence votes at the same time. This may be also for a proper purpose, or it may not be; but generally there is an ulterior purpose.
Why was the money voted last year not expended ? It could not have been for the want of dredging.
I have given all the information at my disposal with regard to this item, and if any further information is required, I will ask that the item stand until further information is brought down.
We had better let it stand. We voted the money last year and none of it was expended. If the work was required at all, and we furnished the money, the government should have expended it.
I think this item had better stand until we find out in what position the work is.
Is the work to be done by day labour ?

No, it is let by contract. My impression at present is, speaking from memory, that this contract was let at the time the Hon. Mr. White represented that constituency. Lot the item stand.
Item allowed to stand.
River St. Lawrence-dredging steamboat channel through shoal at foot of Wolfe Island, $3,000.
The information I have from the chief engineer is that $3,000 will complete a channel 300 feet wide and 10 feet deep. It will complete the work.

Is that being done by government dredge ?
The MINISTER OP PUBLIC WORKS By a hired dredge. Randolph & McDonald are the contractors.
Rondeau harbour-improvements to piers and dredging at entrance, $6,000.

This is to make provision for protecting the west side of the west pier for 1,000 feet in length, also the east pier around its northern end for a distance of 100 feet. The estimated expenditure is $2,100. Nineteen thousand cubic yards of dredging require to be done to make a channel through the bar 1,000 feet long and 10 feet in depth. The chief engineer reports that this amount will be required. There has been already an expenditure of $6,308.35.
What will be done with the $10,000 ?
We ask for a revote of $6,000.
It is not marked here a revote; it is a fresh vote in addition to the $10,000.
The $10,000 will be all spent before the end of the year.
Is this work done by contract ?

By the government dredge ' Ontario.' The piling is done by day labour.
Southampton-improvement of harbour, $10,000.

There has been a good deal of money spent at Southampton. This revote of $10,000 is to be applied to extending the present landing pier in a northern direction for 560 feet, leaving an opening between it and the land for a breakwater of 210 feet, dredging the area thus inclosed to a depth of 17J feet at low water. The depth is 13 feet. Work does not seem to have been carried on there last year. 'Ten thousand dollars was voted and I do not know why the work did not go on last year.
How much money altogether has been spent in the Southampton harbour ?
Since confederation $47,000 have been spent, and previous to that period, about $10,000.

I would like to say with reference to this work, that I have always noticed, whenever there is an election up there, that it is considered very important that there should be some work done at that harbour. The local member, who lives there, is always a very active canvasser, and he assures the people of the importance of sending to Ottawa a supporter of the government in order that money may be spent on that important work. There is nearly always money in the estimates or money on the tapis somewhere or other. If it is necessary to make an expenditure there it should be done. We have had this hanging on year after year. There is no election just now but if there should be one next year it will be a very valuable item to have in the estimates, because it will be made use of- not that I am suggesting that an improper use of it will be made by the department in the way of spending the money-but it will be made use of in the way of influencing the people as to the man they should send down to parliament, because it is desirable to have money spent in this place. Has the government any reasonable expectation of spending the money this year ?

As far as I am concerned I can assure the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) that if the money is not spent this year and if there is not a sufficient excuse to satisfy every hon.

member of this House I will not ask the House to l'evote it. For the want of this pier this harbour has been filling up all the time and boats drawing thirteen or fourteen feet of water cannot get in. It is reported by the chief engineer that if this work is done there will not be the danger of filling up that there has been in the past.
Why was the money not spent last year ?
I cannot answer that.
I have heard it said that even if this pier were placed there the harbour will always fill up. I do not know j if that is correct or not.
Tiie engineer is satisfied that this will prevent it.
How do you propose to do this work ?
It is to be done by contract.
What dredges have you in the Georgian Bay between Parry Harbour and Wiarton, or Southampton ?
Speaking from memory I think there are three or four firms that have dredges there. There is the firm of Porter & Bowman.
But these are not government dredges ?
No, they are not government dredges. We have no government dredges up there just

Before that item passes I would like to say that I quite appreciate the fact that the lion. Minister of Public Works is somewhat handicapped by not having been very long" in the position he is now in, but all the same I think there must be some means of getting a sufficient amount of information to reasonably satisfy this committee. I do not think it will be any excuse to our constituents to go back and tell them that we have not got the information that we should get merely by reason of the fact that there has been a change of portfolios. I am not casting any reflection upon the hon. minister, but speaking in the interest of my own constituents and speaking upon the lines from which the people of the country will judge us, I do say with every confidence, although I have not had a long parliamentary experience, that we of the opposition are bound to get more information than we have been getting before we proceed with these estimates. What position are we in ? The hon. minister tells us candidly night after night virtually that he does not understand the position of these matters that come up for us to pass upon. We ought to have the information. It is true there has been a change of portfolio, but the staff is the same. There is a chief engineer, and if I understand it all correctly, that chief engineer knows a great deal as to the details of the office and as to what is transpiring from time to time. In reference to the matter that is now before us the chief engineer, or some one in the department, surely can tell why it is that it has been delayed. This is of the same class of items as 1 was speaking of a few moments ago. The hon. minister comes to us and tells us that there was a vote last year that was supposed to be for the immediate requirements of the country then, that the money lias not been expended and if there is nothing done I submit to the good sense of the committee on both sides, that it is not sufficient to tell us that it is not known to the department why the money was not expended. The money must be expended because it must not be appropriated unless it is required in the interests of the country. It must be expended or the hon. minister must be prepared to give us some reasonable ground why it has not been expended or to present some exceptional circumstance that has arisen which could not have been foreseen and which has prevented this expenditure. I speak of this item but I could speak of many of the same class and I submit that we of the opposition, who are supposed to be on the alert, who are supposed to watch the expenditure of the administration-and it requires a good deal of watching are bound, whatever courtesy we wish to extend, to require fuller information than we have been afforded in reference to this item.

Mr. Chairman, I have no desire to be excused because I have not been long in the department from furnishing all proper and necessary information. I wish that to be clearly understood. It may he possible that a question may be unexpectedly asked in regard to any work that even the officers of the department could not answer without referring to the papers and books. No minister would be expected to know every possible detail, but as to the general information in reference to this and other votes I think it is unfair to say that I have not furnished the information with the greatest possible detail and if I have not been supplied with all the details by the department T have been willing either to furnish any further information afterwards or to allow the item to stand, as I did in the case of the previous one when I was not satisfied myself that the fullest information had been given. One who has been only a few weeks in the department cannot be as familiar with all these works as a minister who has had them before him on a great many occasions, but

at the same time, no matter how long a minister may have been in the department, he could not be familiar with every detail without reference to the papers and books. I do not think there have been any questions in reference to this item which have not been fully answered excepting the one as to why the money was not spent last year. The officials of the department have too much to do to go on with all the works they have under their care. In some cases it lias been explained that they could not procure the necessary appliances, especially in the case of dredges, to go on with the work. In other cases the reason for delay is that at certain seasons of the year they cannot get people to enter into contracts and they cannot get timber out. I have no desire that any lion, member of the opposition should allow an item to pass without receiving an answer to every reasonable question put to me because it is the duty of the department to furnish ail the information. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lennox) has any questions to ask in connection with the item, other than the one he has referred to. I will be pleased to answer it. I think it is fair to say that I have given the fullest possible information why this vote is asked, what is intended to be done with the money and what object is to be gained by building this pier and continuing the dredging at that point.

There is good cause for complaint because I notice, looking back over the estimates, that this money was voted in 1901-2 and was not spent, and that it was voted in 1902-3 and not spent. Now, we are voting money for 1903-4 and up to the present there has been no expenditure. There seems to be something wrong there.

Since I took office a complaint has been made by the municipal council of the district, but it would appear that the department was not able to cope with all the work it had on hand. This work is undertaken on the report of the engineer that it is urgently necessary, and I pledge myself that it will be proceeded with as quickly ns possible.
Sturgeon Falls-wharf, $4,500.
Lhis wharf is under contract, the contract price being $2,S00 and the contractor is Robert Grant, of Toronto.
Is this the Grant that is figuring m the Stratton case ?
I think this Mr. Grant is a contractor and an honest man.
Has the town provided the site?

The right of way was purchased by the Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
municipality and transferred to the Crown free.

What was the value of
the land ?
I do not know what] they paid for it.
Is this on the river or on the lake ?
It is on Sturgeon river and quite a business is done there.
Does this wharf serve a local purpose only; is there any navigation up and down the river ?

It must be largely for local shipping. The information furnished me is that twelve or thirteen steamboats use this wharf, the largest having a draft of eight feet and Sturgeon river is navigable for vessels of that size a distance of four miles to Lake Nipissiug.
What is the ordinary line of business which Mr. Grant is engaged in ?
I have not a personal acquaintance with Mr. Grant, but perhaps the hon. member for Toronto knows him. I understand he is a contractor of considerable experience.
I thought he was a lawyer.
All the better if he were.
There is a gentleman Robert Grant, a contractor in Toronto. There used to be a gentleman of that name having contracts with the city. I do not know much about him.

When we have painters and newspaper men and lawyers turning up as government contractors it looks rather suspicious. They often farm out the business and have a rake off. I thought perhaps that might be so in this case. Was there more than one tender ?

I think there were seven. There is a good deal of competition in these small works. Mr. Grant was the lowest tenderer. I am informed this vote will complete the work.
Thornbury-repairs to harbour works, $1,500. Mr. SPROULE. Are you doing any dredging here? I understand that some dredging is required, but if you have to repair the pier out of this vote as well, there will not be much left for dredging. [DOT]
The department did some dredging there last year.
am informed that some dredging is required there yet.
1 expect there will be and if so I will have to get another vote.

I may say with regard to this vote and the vote for Meaford that a much larger expenditure is necessary than you have provided for in the estimates. Do you intend to ask a further sum in the supplementary estimates ? I know that you can expend money to good advantage there and the people would not be displeased if there was a much larger expenditure than you apparently contemplated.

The mayor and the municipal council of Meaford have made strong representations to me by petiton and the chief engineer is now up there examining the place. I will be governed by his report as to what further work shall be done there this year.
Toronto harbour-works at eastern entrance, $14,000.
The' Postmaster General is probably much interested in this work, aud if it is -agreeable to the minister I would ask that this vote be deferred until Sir William Mulock is in the House.
This work has no connection with the matters to which the Toronto deputation made reference recently. I had a communication from the council this week pointing out that this work is very pressing.
Will there be another item for Toronto ?
I hope so.
Then we could discuss that question on that other item. If that is understood I will not object.

Yes, the matter can be discussed on any item for public works. I am furnished with the following information with regard to this particular work. This is for the construction of two groynes to protect the island shore at an estimated cost of some $3,000; rebuilding and stone ballasting breakwater, $3,500; repairs to superstructure of eastern channel piers, $4,000. My hon. friend will notice that these are small works which if' neglected would cost a great deal more a few months from now.
Is this work being done by contract or by day labour ?
All by contract.

I notice by the Auditor General's Report for 1901-2, at page Y-273, that one of the foremen on this work is Frank J. Sullivan. Is this the Sullivan who is under suspicion at the present time in
connection with the Stratton-Gamey investigation ?
I have no information as to that, but I shall be pleased to make inquiries and let the hon. gentleman know.

The entry is :	' Frank J.
Sullivan, foreman, and nine men, one half day, putting government derrick scow in water, $15.' I am informed it is the same man who was in the employ of the government and recently resigned.
Trenton dredging-Trent river, $5,000.
I would like to ask the minister where this dredging is to be done ?

This is a revote for the purpose of removing small stones and gravel and providing a channel of sufficient depth. The reason of the delay was that the department could not secure a dredge to go on with the work.

How is it that the public works of this country are so delayed for the want of dredges ? There was a time in the history of Ontario not long ago when there were plenty of dredges. Is it because there are some parties the government do not want to employ to do the dredging ? I know that it used to be said that shoemakers got contracts for dredging, and then hired somebody to do the work and made a rake-off. I never knew that there were not dredges "enough to do the work, yet we have thousands of dollars voted and not expended because we are told there are not enough dredges.

I may say as a matter of fact there are no dredges procurable, though at some points there may be too many. We have a dredge almost completed which will, I hope, early this season be placed on this section to complete this work.
Wendover wharf, $t,000.
The minister is asking for $1,000 this year, and last year we voted $3,000. I would ask him if the contract has been let, and how the work is being done ?
No, this was done by day's labour under the superintendence of one of the engineers of the department.
How much was spent last year ?
Three thousand and eighty dollars has been spent in the current year.

I find at page Y-273 and 274 of the Auditor General's Report that there was expended on the Wendover wharf

last year $6,502.22. Was tills the beginning of tlie expenditure, or was there an expenditure before that ?
That was the first work done.
Where is Wendover ?
Oil the Ottawa river.

Does the minister know anything about the population of the place, or whose riding it is in ?
The S1INISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. This wharf affords landing and shipping facilities to the residents of Wendover and the farmers of the vicinity. The nearest communication by rail is nine miles.

I desire to call attention to this subject because it raises a question that was very much discussed last year. The minister last year obtained an appropriation of $3,000, and expended more than double the money authorized by parliament. We were assured that that would not occur again. The subject was discussed in the Public Accounts Committee, and the Auditor General said that he had brought the attention of the government to it, and that it would not occur again. I think parliament is entitled to more consideration from the departments than that. A department brings in an estimate to cover the cost of a particular work, a vote is taken for it, tuid then, utterly regardless of the amount authorized by parliament, the department spends more than double the amount authorized, and then comes back in the following year and asks for more money. I do not think that is treating parliament in the way in which it is entitled to be treated.

T think the hon. gentleman has overlooked the fact that the first vote for this work was taken in 1901-2. The vote for 1902-3 was $3,000. That amount has been spent, and now, to complete the work, $1,000 is required. I do not see anything irregular in the expenditure. I am not aware what estimate was given by the minister at first. There may have been an under estimate, but It is not a very serious one, because according to the report of the engineer this $1,000 will complete the work.

The hon. gentleman may not think it is a serious difference when the expenditure is more than 100 per cent above what was authorized, but I do consider it a serious difference. Three thousand dollars was all the minister was authorized to spend at Wendover. He spent $6,500 there, and now he is asking for another $1,000.
My hon. friend is mistaken as to this vote. He must be referring to the vote of 1901-2.
I am reading from the hon. gentleman's estimates. He wants a thousand dollars for this year. He states in the other columns that the amount authorized last year was three thousand dollars.
Yes.
That is for the expenditure last year. Yet according to the Auditor General's Report, he expended $6,500.
My hon. friend has made a slight error. The fiscal year ends the 30th of June next
I am aware of that.
The Auditor General's Report refers to the appropriation expended in the year 1901-2. Tlie $3,000 was voted for the year 1902-3. I have not at my hand just now what the amount voted for 1901-2 was.
The Auditor General's Report is for the expenditure of the year ending 30th June, 1902.

That was for the appropriation voted for
1901-	2. It does not refer to this $3,000 at all.

We have for the year
1902-	3 the sum of $3,000. If the hon. minister is correct quite a sum will be spent on this work. Where is the village of Wendover and why should such an amount be spent upon a wharf which can only accommodate local traffic. I know of no stretch on the Ottawa so important that we should have that amount spent upon it from year to year.
My hon. friend must see that during the session of 1901-2, parliament must have voted at least $7,000 to begin this work. In the session of 1902-3 parliament voted $3,000 more, making $10,000.
Has that been spent ?
Yes, and I am asking for $1,000 to complete the work.

How was that $3,000 spent

by contract or by day labour ?
By day labour.
How many foremen had you there ?
Only one. It was done under the superintendence of the resident engineer.

As I have already pointed out, there was an expenditure for the year 1901-2, as recorded in the Auditor General's Report, of $6,500. The hon. minister ex-

in seeing that such unauthorized expenditures are not still going on.

I notice that this item is in three different parts-ice-breakers, storehouse and waiting room. How is it divided? What proportion will be spent on ice-breakers ? What is the size of the waiting room, and what will it cost ?
The ice-breakers are for the protection of the wharf. The waiting room is a small part of tlie warehouse partitioned off for the accommodation of the people waiting for the boats.

I would like to have from the Minister of Public Works an expression
plained that that would not touch the $3,000 appropriation which we voted last year; but looking at the estimates for the year 1901-2, there does not appear to be any appropriation at all for Wendover in those estimates. Will the hon. minister tell us that it is in the supplementary estimates, because otherwise there would not appear to be any appropriation at all.
There must have been a vote at least of $0,500 or the department could not have spent the money in 1901-2, and the Auditor General would not have sanctioned the expenditure.
Last year we found over and over again that money was expended away beyond the estimate without the authority of parliament at all.

What the hon. gentleman says is begging the question. He says that as we do not find the item in the general estimates and we do not find an expenditure of $0,500, it must follow that the vote was in the supplementary estimate.
I did not say that. I said that there must have been an appropriation or the department could not have spent the money, and the Auditor General would not have passed upon the expenditure.

We ought to know whether there was a vote for this expenditure or not, especially in view of the fact, to which my hon. friend from Hamilton has drawn attention, that time and again we have found expenditures which have ex-ceded the appropriation.
I have here the supplementary and the general estimates for 1901-2 and this place does not appear in either.
If my hon. friend will look at the Supply Bill on page 41 he will find a vote of $6,500.
Is that in the estimates ?

It is in the statutes on page 41. I think that I am perfectly right in saying the Auditor General would not account for an expenditure of $6,500 unless the money had been spent and gone through the regular channels.

Perhaps the hon. minister j is not aware of what has been done in some qf the departments. I can only tell him an actual fact, that last year the Public Accounts Committee investigated a case where $8,000 had been granted to parliament for a particular work and more than double that sum had been expended, and the Auditor General said he would see that It would not occur again. We are justified
of opinion as to the policy of such items as this. Leaving aside, for the moment, the question to which I have directed attention more than once in this committee the undesirability of building local wharfs all over the country. I would like to know if it is the policy of the administration to build not only wharfs but warehouses, and not only warehouses, but waiting rooms for all the hamlets and at the mouths of all the small streams in the country. I understand from the hon. minister that this place is nine miles from a railway station. That may be a reason why the public of that neighbourhood require a wharf and a store house and a waiting room. But there is a great distinction between ascertaining that that is necessary for the accommodation of the people of the locality and coming to the conclusion that it is the duty of the government, of the Dominion, at the expense of the whole of Canada, to supply that local accommodation. If this is the policy of this government, I protest against such a system of spending the public money of the Dominion. It may be a perfectly legitimate expenditure of money for some authority, but it is an unjustifiable expenditure, I submit, of the money of the Dominion of Canada.
It is not customary to build warehouses on these wharfs. I believe. Will the minister please explain the necessity for it in this case ?
I believe that on most of the wharfs the government puts up a warehouse or some kind of shelter for goods. As to the waiting room, it is merely a part of the warehouse partitioned off.

I thouglft that the warehouses were usually built by the iocnlitv. On the Georgian Bay at Thornbury, for instance, while the dock was built by the government, the warehouse was built by the municipality. I think the same is true of Meaford.

There is no rule in the matter. In many cases private individuals have their warehouses alongside the docks, but in small

places like this the government huilds, in connection with the dock a small, cheap frame warehouse.
There ought to be some rule that would apply equally to all places. Otherwise, you do too much for one place and not enough for another.
Is there a village where this wharf is ? Is there a post office there ?
There is a small village. I have not a memorandum of the population. The wharf is quite a little distance from the village.
When this item was first introduced, what was this work supposed to cost ?
I cannot answer that, as the estimate is not before me. The estimate of what it would cost should have been given three years ago when this vote was first taken.
I have examined the records, and I find no account of them.

I confess I cannot see why the Dominion should furnish not only a wharf, but a warehouse and a waiting room at a point where the population is so small that, if we may trust the Postmaster General's Report, there is not even a post office there. It appears to me that there must be something behind this vote that is not honest. I feel convinced of that. I do not think the Minister of Public Works himself feels easy in his conscience in making this expenditure.
Who is in charge of this storehouse and waiting room ?
The Department of Marine and Fisheries always appoint a wharfinger to take charge of these public wharfs.
Who owns this wharf ?
The government.
How can we find out who is appointed to take charge, for the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Prfi-fontaine) is not here ?

The .Minister of Public Works, I must say, is usually pretty candid in telling us wh#t he intends to do in future in regard to these matters. Already during the discussion of these estimates I think he has upon more than one occasion indicated that there will be a substantial improvement in the conduct of the department in the future, that better methods will be adopted. I was in hopes that he would tell us that, whether the larger improvement I have been urging, the total abandonment of this system of local improvements at the expenses of the exchequer, was to be adopt-

ed or not, at all events, we might look for such an improvement as would prevent, in the future, expenditures for waiting rooms. If the minister will tell us thatL it would be some assurance that matters "would be improved. Now, assuming that it was proposed to put up that little building at the expense of the township in which it is situated, to accommodate people within a range of seven, or eight, or nine miles, could it be contended that it was a proper expenditure of the money of the township or of the money of the county ? I think that could not be contended, much less, then, could it be contended that it is proper to expend the money of the Dominion of Canada for the same purpose. I say it should be observed as a principle that we should not have any longer this system of expending public money. The hon. member for Grey spoke of it as an injustice ; I say it is more than an injustice, I say that this money cannot be expended at Wendover for the purpose of building a warehouse and be an honest expenditure of the money of this country. I contend that when the work is so local in its character as not to justify the expenditure of money by the municipality, it is manifest that an expenditure of money by the Dominion for the same purpose is much less justifiable.

This is certainly a surprise to me. I was aware that a great number of new wharfs were being erected in various towns and small villages throughout the country; but I never knew before that either this or any former administration erected storehouses and waiting rooms for the benefit! of private individuals. According to the information before us, this storehouse and waiting room have been erected, and we cannot find out now who is in charge of the property. Property of that kind left without some one being in charge, will soon become useless. It seems to me we should have more information in regard to this particular case. I do not think the minister is prepared to say that he has any precedent for this kind of thing. Certainly, I do not know of a single instance where this or any other administration has expended public money in erecting storehouses and waiting rooms of this character.
There are dozens and dozens of precedents for this expenditure, ever since confederation. It is usual to erect warehouses for the accommodation of the produce of people at these wharfs.
Who is responsible for the safe keeping of these places, generally ?

As I explained, when a wharf is built by the Public Works Department it is transferred to the care of the Marine Department, who appoints the wharfinger. But

that cannot affect the expenditure in any way. If my hon. friend wishes to know the name of the wharfinger, he can get it when the Marine estimates are under consideration.
Will the minister inform us who is the gentleman that asked for this work to be done ?

This House authorized an expenditure on this work three years ago, and all the information should have been furnished then. A year ago we had a vote of $3,000, and I am now asking, on the advice of the engineer, for $1,000 for the purpose of building this work. If it were a new work, that I was asking for, of course the responsibility that would devolve upon me of giving the information would be very different from what it is now. Parliament has committed itself to this work, and the money has been spent, with the exception of a small amount.
Did the engineer recommend this work in the first place ?
Surely parliament did not allow the item to pass three years ago without this information.

Questions were asked when this vote was brought down, but no information was given. That is the trouble we have had right along. When there is any reference to the past record we cannot find any information in it.

I have said on previous occasions that I disapproved of parliament being asked for a vote without full information of the probable cost. I am no more accountable for this than the hon. gentleman, and perhaps not so much. I agree that the officers of the department should furnish the minister and he should furnish parliament with an estimate of the total cost of any work before it is undertaken. Any over estimate or under estimate would have to be accounted for to the satisfaction of parliament. In this case, if that was omitted, I suppose we are all responsible.
I draw attention to the fact that we have no record of what the work has cost or any other information about it. The hon. gentleman himself is not in a position to give us the information.
The hon. gentleman for the first time, probably, has got the information. I have given him now full information as to the cost.
The estimated cost of the work ?

No, the actual cost, what has been spent 46
and what it will take to complete. The hon. gentleman has not been paying attention to the discussion.
The minister forgets that when this item was brought in at first there was nothing to show what the original estimate was. That is what we are asking the hon. gentleman for.
There was none.
No original estimate for this work ? That is a bad give-away, for the department.
Is there no report from an engineer or some official recommending it, showing a public necessity for this work? The minister might give us that information.
Mr. Michaud, one of the engineers, did make a report in 1901, estimating the cost of this work at $7,000.
That information, apparently, was not given to the committee at first.
Apparently not.
On what ground was the work recommended ? Was there any clamour for it among the people living down there, any public demand for the construction of this work ?

I will be pleased to look over the files of the department for the past three years and see what applications were made and if there were any petitions from the people there, or other papers, in connection with this work. With the permission of the committee we might go back to the item of $4,000 for the improvement of the Narrows at Pete-wawa above Pembroke. I have the information now that the work costs about $7,000. The work has been done and the money was to be paid under the contract on the completion of the work. The reason it was not paid was that there was a dispute between the contractor, Mr. W. J. Poupore and the department as to the completion of the work. The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) asked me why that item was revoted. There is a dispute between the contractor and the department as to whether the work has been completed according to the contract or not. That accounts for revoting the money.
Have you come to a settlement yet ?
Not yet.

I would like to ask the hon. minister if the work of dredging along the River St. Lawrence, at Wolfe



Island, and other places is to be done by day's work or by tender ?
That work was done by contract. The dredge which did the work was the property of Mr. Macdonald.
At what rate was it engaged ?
At $8 an hour.
Does that include tugs and scows ?
Yes.
Is that a fair charge ?

It is supposed to be a fair charge. It has been the charge for several years in the department. I do not know whether we will be able to continue that. Applications have been made for increased wages and the cost of everything has been increased. That has been the price for a great many years for a dredge of the minimum capacity of 600 cubic yards.
I suppose there is a fair wage officer to look after all these things ?
That is for a small sized dredge.
The report of the department shows that that is a dredge of the capacity of 600 yards a day.
What rate do you pay for a large sized dredge ?
From $10 to $12 per hour and as high as $15.
Is that the highest price that the department has paid for a dredge ?
So far as the memory of the deputy minister goes he thinks that $15 is the highest.
Is that for a large sized dredge ?
Yes.
And that includes scows, tugs and all complete ?
That includes all the apparatus.

What was the contract price for that work at the narrows at Pete-wawa ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS $7,000.
Was there any more money expended on it than the contract price ?
Nothing has been paid by the department yet.
Will that finish the work ?
There is a dispute between the contractor and the department as to this work. The contractor claims that it cost him a great deal more to do the work.
How did he do it ?
By blasting and dredging.
Was there a signed contract ?
Yes.
Is that work completed now ? I do not think it is.
It is a question in dispute between the contractor and the department as to whether it is completed or not.
The work is not completed. I was there last year. There is no use saying it is. The work is not completed.
If the hon. member (Hon. Mr. Tarte) had been present he would have known that was what I explained.
I would like to know if it is completed or not.
Not according to the contention of the department.

There are not two ways of interpreting that contract. The work is not completed. The contractor had made a contract with the late government for a certain sum of money. He has been going on very slowly indeed. I was there last year and I say it again the work is not completed. But of course I may say immediately that the work cannot be completed for the sum for which it was agreed to do it. It is out of the question. The work is worth, I believe, about twice as much as the price of the contract. These are the facts of the case. The work is not done. There is only part of it done.
I would like to ask the hon. minister what it costs per day to run one of his dredges. What does it cost to run one of the large sized dredges like ' J. I. Tarte ' for instance ?

That is an important matter not connected with this work and when the vote for dredg-

mg is up I would rather bring down the figures and furnish all the information. Roughly, I should say about $200 per day.
In an off-hand statement of that kind I suppose you include tugs, scows, dredges, coal and wages ?
I do not think they have any scows with that dredge.
You must have scows to take away what you dredge ?
No.
Take one of your large dredges in connection with which you use scows-do you include scows, tugs, coal and everything connected with it ?
It would not be nearly as much for one of the smaller dredges.	*
But take one of your chief dipper dredges with which you use scows and tugs-roughly, what would it cost per day to handle a dredge of that kind ?
I would not like to speak from memory.
The officer of the department knows roughly.
Perhaps from $100 to $125 per day.
That would include everything ?
Yes.

Returning to that Pembroke dredging item the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) gives the committee some light by making the statement that it will cost double the amount of the contract. Will the hon. minister tell the committee if it is the intention of the government to go on and complete the work, if they make a settlement with the contractor ?

I should not be bound by what I say here, because the matter was only brought to my attention a few days ago. The contract was made by the previous government with Mr. Poupore according to the specifications. The officers of the department claim that this work has not been completed under the specifications under which he took that contract. It will cost no doubt a great deal more money to complete this work according to specifications. He has furnished accounts to the department already for some $14,000. If the shoal is so removed as to furnish at low water a sufficient depth for boats to navigate there, I am inclined to think it would be better to make a settlement with Mr. Poupore than to go on spending 46*
money on this work. One of the engineers of the department has recently reported to the effect that there is eight feet of water at the shoal.
Which engineer made that report ?
Mr. Fraser.
When did he make the survey ?
Within the last two or three weeks.
We have no information as to what kind of a contract this was. Was it a contract to give a certain depth of water; was it to take out so many cubic yards, or was it to remove the shoal ?
The late governmet made a contract with Mr. Poupore to do this work.
What kind of a contract?

As I understand it, he undertook to remove this shoal for $7,000, There has been a dispute ever since between Mr. Poupore and the department as to whether the work has been done according to contract.
What were the specifications ? It might take $100,000 to remove a shoal and it might only take $5,000. Surely the contract must have been let in some intelligent way.
There was a plan furnished by the engineer, and the contractor undertook to do the work for $7,000.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) can move for the papers and get all the information. It was so much money for so much work to give us so many feet of water. The truth of the matter is that the contractor sent in a tender which was far too low, and the contract has been dragging along for eight or ten years. That is the whole thing in two words. The price he tendered at was twice too low, and he cannot complete the work for the money. There is about eight feet of water now, and it is considered by certain parties that that is enough, but nevertheless the contract has not been carried out. It would take $15,000 instead of $7,000. The question came before me, and I had nothing else to do than to tell the contractor to carry out his contract, and when the work was completed I would pay him. The work was not completed when I left office and I did not pay him.

Well, that gives us some additional information, but surely before the department let the contract it had an engineer's estimate, and it would not let a work at less than half the actual cost. There was something wrong about the de-

partment or the engineer, or they would not get into a tangle like that.

The contractor claims that when he did tender he did not receive from the department all the information he should have had. He thinks there was a mistake made, but at all events he has acted in good faith.-

The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) says that if I want the information I can move for the papers. It is the duty of the minister who is asking us to vote money to provide us with all necessary information which would satisfy us whether it is wise or not to vote the money, and it is not our business to go around the departments looking for information. This item should stand until we get this information.
What information does the hon. gentleman want ?
I want to know what kind of a contract was made with Mr. Pou-pore. I have not been able to ascertain yet what kind of a contract it was.

I thought I had given all that information, but probably it would be better to strike the item out. This is a disputed account between the department and Mr. Poupore. It arose under the late government, and when the matter came before me some time ago I was inclined to think that it would be better to come to some conclusion on it. Mr. Poupore claims he has done the work as he understood it, (but the engineer reports differently to the department, and the ex-minister says he went on the engineer's report and he would not pay Mr. Poupore. My suggestion under these circumstances is to strike the item out, and I will bring down all the papers in connection with it, and if that is satisfactory to the House we can put another item in the estimates. If there is sufficient water for the boats that navigate the river there we might probably pay Mr. Poupore what the officials think would be fair for the work he has done. I do not suppose that any member of this House wants a contractor to do work for nothing. I think that will be the better way. I move that this item be struck out, and I will bring down a vote in the supplementary estimates for the settlement of this matter, and will then give full particulars to the Committee.
I do not see why the ,tem should be struck out, because there is certainly more money now due for work done than the amount in the estimates.
I agree with my'hon. friend, but I think this is the better way to deal with the matter. It is an old claim, the work has been done, but the engineers think not according to the contract.
Motion agreed to, and item struck out.
Manitoba-harbours, rivers and bridges-general repairs and improvements, $3,000.
This is a general vote for extraordinary repairs.

One of our members who wished to be here when these items on Manitoba went through is away, and if it would not be interfering with the order of work too much, I would suggest that the hon. minister take some other items and leave one for discussion.
Leave the particular item the hon. gentleman refers to, and pass the balance of the estimates.

I think the suggestion of the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) is the better one. It is a small vote, and we will pass all the items except one, on which any item can be discussed.
Gull harbour, St. George's bay-extension of wharf, $1,500.
This is a revote to pay for the extension of this wharf 50 feet.
Is this work done by contract ?

No, by day labour.
Hnausa-wharf extension, $1,500.
This is to complete this work.
Is that being done by day labour as well ?

Yes. This is a wharf of considerable size. It was originally built by contract, but these repairs are being done by day labour.
Lake Dauphin-lowering of, $5,000.
Mi'. REID (Grenville). Is this work done by dredging ?
There is no provision made for a dredge there yet. The intention of the department is either to build or acquire a small dredge to go on with this necessary work.
How much land do you expect to reclaim by lowering the waters of that lake ?

The report of the engineer does not give the quantity of land. It is estimated that the total cost of the work will be $9,000, We have not yet been able to procure a dredge, and the engineer is now building a small one for this-work.
The water overflows the land for a distance of six or seven miles from the lake shore. On this account many settlers had to leave there some years ago.

I understood that if this j Jake were dredged, a large acreage of land which is now practically useless, would he reclaimed and made available for agricultural purposes. I have no doubt the money is needed and it is desirable to do the work, but I think the department ought to provide some way of doing it. We do not want tills money to be voted from year to year for a quarter of a century without the work being done.

My information from the engineer is that he is going to do the work this season.
Lake Manitoba-additional outlet via Fairford river, $5,000.
This vote is to be applied to the removal of boulders from the bed of the river in order to regulate the flow from lake Manitoba.
Did you do any tvork last year ?

No, there has been no work done there, owing to the very high water during the summer of 1902 and the want of a suitable dredging plant. The engineer reports that for $3,000 we could build a dredge.
Lake Francis outlet, Manitoba-construction of piers and dredging, $6,000.

Orders have been given to go on with this work and make provisions for a permanent outlet for Lake Francis on the eastern shore of Lake Manitoba. We expect to do that work between now and the 30th of June.
Has the hon. minister obtained any statement from the engineer that this money will complete the work.
We have a report from Mr. Miall, the engineer for the department, that $8,500 will do this work.
Complete it fully ?

That is the report of the engineer. Of course in large works covering such an area, the minister must depeud on the report of his engineer. That is the only information that in most cases the minister and parliament can have to depend upon.

No doubt the minister must be guided by his engineers and nobody will find fault with a trifling discrepancy between the engineer's estimate and the cost of the work when Anally completed. But we find frequently the department entering on a large work without the slightest idea of where it is going to land them. Thousands of dollars are spent beyond the original estimate when, if parliament knew at the beginning what expenditure was involved, parliament would never have authorized the undertaking. The minister should always be able to show that he has his engineer's written report, stating what the whole work will cost from beginning to end. Whether that report be thoroughly reliable or not is another question, but he ought to have it.

I quite agree with my hon. friend, and my policy is to submit these reports on all occasions before a work is begun.
Selkirk, Manitoba-extension of wharf, $3,000.

This is to complete the 300 feet addition to Selkirk wharf. The work was begun in 1902-3, and will cost about $6,000 altogether
Wharf at Lake Winnipeg at Gimli-to complete repairs, $1,250.

This is to complete. The total cost is $4,940. It is being done by day's work.
White Mnd river-dredging at mouth of, $3,500.
Have you a dredge there?
Yes, and the work is going on this season.
What is the full cost of tlie work ?
The total expenditure so far is $29,578, and the report of the engineer is that $3,500 are necessary to continue the work this year.
Where is White Mud river ?
In Macdonald county.
Is this place navigable ? And how many vessels approach that wharf ?

There are many vessels plying on Lake Manitoba, and they have great difficulty in finding shelter. By dredging this river, vessels will be able to find a harbour some three miles up from the lake. The Northern Pacific put on a steamer at the foot of the lake, when they completed their road, and both steamer and wharf were entirely washed away.
North-west Territories-harbours, rivers and bridges, including approaches-general repairs and improvements, $5,000.
Surely the minister is going to ask for the appropriation of more money than this for the territories ?
This vote is only for extraordinary cases of repairs and so on. There will be separate votes for other works.
This has nothing to do with the territorial vote ?
No, it is a general vote.	[DOT]

Though it does not relate to the item immediately under discussion, I would like to take advantage of the opportunity to draw attention to a statement that appears in the Montreal ' Star ' to-night, to the effect that a great many of the colonists going out to the Rev. Mr. Barr's settlement will suffer great hardship in travelling the road from Saskatoon to their settlement. As a matter of fact, the road referred to is better than most of the streets in Ottawa, better than most of roads in England. These settlers will suffer no hardship so far as the roads are concerned over which they must travel to their colony. I think it very unfortunate that erroneous statements such as this to which I refer should appear in the press. Settlers who came into Ontario in the old days suffered greater hardships in two miles of road than these Barr colonists will have to undergo in their whole journey.
British Columbia-Anderson and Kennedy lakes-clearing outlets, $2,500.
This is to complete the removal of boulders and other obstructions at the outlets of these lakes.
How is this work to be done ?

By day labour.
Columbia river, above Revelstoke-removal of obstructions to navigation, $6,000.
Where is this ?
This is to be applied in continuing the work of removing dangerous points of rocks, reefs and boulders from the bed of the river over a distance of fifty miles between Revelstoke and Death's Rapids.
How is the work to be done, by contract ?
It is to be done under the supervision of the resident engineer for British Columbia.
Who is he '!
Mr. Keefer.

I would like to draw attention to correspondence which was printed in the ' News Advertiser ' on the 30th of November, 1902, respecting the treatment meted out to Mr. D. Sinclair, who had been in charge of some work in British Columbia under the Public Works Department.
Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) allow me to say that that was not in connection with the works now under discussion. That will come up under an item later on.

I asked the minister how the work under discussion was to be done, and he informed me it would be under the supervision of the resident engineer, Mr. Keefer. I was going to read for the information of the hon. minister and the committee a letter alleged to have been written by the resident engineer to a gentleman named Sinclair.
I have no objection, but if Mr. Sinclair was doing work in connection with another vote, perhaps it might be more properly discussed under' that vote.
That was on the Salmon river, which will come up later. Perhaps the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) will take it up when we reach that item.
Where is the item for work on the Salmon river ?
I find that there is no special vote for the Salmon river.
I shall be delighted to defer to the wishes of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Gallilier) if he will tell me under what item I shall bring this matter up.
Right here, if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) wishes it.

That will be quite satisfactory to me. I bring this forward because I wish to know under what system the public works in British Columbia are being carried on. I cannot vouch for the accuracy of the statements in the article I refer to, but it is only right that I should let the hon. minister and the representative of the district! have an opportunity of saying whether these statements are correct or not. This is what is represented to have appeared in the * News Advertiser ' on the 30th of November, 1902 :

Abuse of a Bad System.
Kamloops, Nov. 27.-Mr. D. Sinclair, who has been in charge of the Dominion improvement work at Salmon Arm, has been dismissed because, as correspondence shows-not having received any such instructions from his chief. Dominion Resident Engineer Keefer-he did not discharge some of the good workers he had employed and substitute for them nominees of a man named McGuire, who acts as secretary of the Liberal Association at Salmon Arm. The letter of dismissal ran thus :
New Westminster, B.C., October 3, 1902.
Sir,-I regret that, at the request of Mr. W. A. Galliher, M.P., I have to request that you hand over the charge of the work of improvement of Salmon river to Mr. G. McLeod. I do not know what the trouble is, but my instructions from Ottawa are to defer to the wishes of the local member in the appointment of men on the government work in their respective districts, and in the purchase of supplies. As far as I am aware, your work of last year was

well done, so it is not on the score of incompetence that you are superseded.
Yours faithfully,
G. A. KEEFER, Resident Engineer. Mr. D. Sinclair, Salmon Arm, B.C.
I would like to ask the minister whether instructions were issued from the department to Mr. Keefer respecting the discharge and employment of men under the department in British Columbia, whether the statement X have quoted is a truthful one and whether instructions were issued to discharge this gentleman who, as Mr. Keefer himself alleges, had done his work faithfully and in a competent manner and to employ only men nominated by the member for the district? Is it the policy of the government and is it the intention of the minister that work in British Columbia or any other province shall be doue in this way ? I think we should have a statement from the lion, minister on this subject.
This matter has never been brought to my attention. The deputy minister tells me that he knows nothing about it.
We might have the correspondence brought down.
I think it would be better. I have not seen the article that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) has quoted, nor do I know anything about it.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman (Mr. Galliher) who represents the district might explain the matter.

As the representative of that district, I know the facts. Also, I am responsible, if any one is responsible, for having Mr. Sinclair discontinued as foreman of that work. The circumstances are these : There was an appropriation in 1901 of $2,500 for clearing out this river. I recommended Mr. Sinclair as foreman for 1901, and ho acted as foreman in clearing out that river in 1901. In 1902 there was a further appropriation of $2,500 for clearing that river, and a foreman was appointed for that year. The resident engineer, Mr. Keefer, asked Sinclair to go to work without consulting me-I don't blame him, because I suppose, as there was no kick about Mr. Sinclair's work for the preceding year, he probably thought it would be all right to continue him for the second year. But Mr. Sinclair had no appointment from the government or anybody else for the second year. That letter was written by Mr. Keefer to him. Now, along that river there are a number of settlers, men who are trying to hew out for themselves a home in that valley along the river. It was my desire that the benefit of any moneys expended on that river should be given to these settlers rather than to men whose occupation was loafing around town. I was
informed that Mr. Sinclair was taking charge of that work for the second year, that is for 1902, and that he was not carrying out my wishes in that respect. I telegraphed to Mr. Sinclair asking him to follow my instructions, as it was my desire that the settlers who were there as bona fide settlers should receive the benefit of that money, and I drew no distinction between friends and enemies in that respect. Mr. Sinclair treated my telegram very cavalierly, saying he was not taking instructions from Mr. Galliher. The result was that in two days he was not taking instructions from anybody, somebody else was attending to that work.
Hear, hear.
I ask any hon. gentleman on that side to say if he would have acted differently.
I would think it was an impertinence to act in that way.

Well, your ideas and mine differ. Those are the circumstances of the case, the circumstances under which that man was dismissed, because he was not rightly there for the year 1902. He had taken over that work, he was assuming to act there as foreman without having received an appointment from the department. His appointment was not a continuing appointment while that river required clearing, his appointment was only for the year 1901.
Might I ask the hon. gentleman when the work commenced in 1902 ?
Some time in the fall.
The letter is dated 2nd of October, I think.
Some time in the fall. I know I went up on the work myself in November, while it was continuing.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman would tell us whom he employed instead of this man, and what he paid him.
Instead of this man I recommended that a Mr. McLeod be apoint-ed, and his pay was exactly that of Mr. Sinclair's.

I would draw the attention of the committee to the fact that we were told by the minister that the work in British Columbia was done under the directions or instructions of the resident engineer, Mr. Keefer. Now I have presented to the House his letter to Mr. Sinclair. Of course, I am bound to accept the statement of the hon. member from Cariboo (Mr. Galliher) but there seems to be discrepancy between the statement of the minister and that made by the hon. gentleman. 1 was aware of the fact that Mr. Keefer has no authority, unless instructions are received from the department or from the representative of the district, to employ the

men. He makes the statement that Mr. Sinclair's work was satisfactorily done in 1901.
No dispute about that.
And that be was dismissed because instructions had been received from the local member to dismiss him. Is that practice going to prevail in the future in British Columbia or elsewhere ?

It has always been the practice, when the chief engineer is asking for the appointment of a foreman, to take the recommendation of the member for the riding. I do not think there is anything wrong in that.
Did he take his instructions direct from the hon. member ?
Certainly not. The hon. member explained that he did not recommend this man, and did not consider that the chief engineer had any right to appoint him.
But the hon. member ordered his dismissal, and he was dismissed within two days.
If the hon. member will pardon me-I made a distinction when I said that for 1902 he was not appointed foreman by the department. Therefore he was not dismissed as a matter of fact.
The hon. member made the statement that Mr. Sinclair was on duty, and he recommended Mr. Sinclair as the man in charge.
I did not.

He wrote to Mr. Sinclair giving him instructions what he was to do as concerns the engaging of the men, and Mr. Sinclair replied that he was not taking orders from him, and that within two days he was not taking orders' from anybody. Therefore, I would understand that he issued instructions that this man must be dismissed, and that the department acted accordingly.

When I received word that Mr. Sinclair was not carrying out my wishes in the matter with regard to the employment of settlers on this work, I then took objection to his being foreman for the year 1902. Mr. Sinclair was not appointed foreman by the department for the year 1902 ; and although, as I say, the resident engineer, presuming perhaps that he was right in doing so, presuming that because his work had been satisfactory in the year before, it would be all right to continue him for 1902, asked him to go to work. Yet l did not consider that as an appointment, it was not an appointment by the department.
The hon. member overlooks the statement made by the minister a few minutes ago. When asked how this
work was done in British Columbia, he said it was done under the instructions of the resident engineer, who had control of it.
Under his supervision.

A very different thing. The work is done under the supervision of the engineer, that is, the engineer has the right to say how, where and when that work should be done. That is what I understand by the supervision of the engineer. I do not think it is the engineer's duty to appoint the foreman, or to hire the men, either.

I consider this man was an officer of the department and was appointed by the department, since they paid him. Now this man was foreman during 1901, at least, he was paid regularly and monthly by the department. Then he must have been appointed by the department.
That is true for 1901.
Then he must have been recognized by the hon. member as the officer in charge.
For that year and no other.

The point I am getting at is this : I would like to know from the hon. member the day he was dismissed. The hon. member says the department dismissed him on his telegram, he was dismissed within forty-eight hours.
I did not say forty-eight hours.
The bon. member said within two days.
I should have said a few days.

I think the minister should tell us how this man was dismissed, because this is a very important matter as regards appointments elsewhere. Here is a man doing his duty, the hon. member admits that he did his work satisfactorily and honestly during 1901 ; and simply because he was not carrying out his instructions, but was carrying out the instructions of the department, he is dismissed promptly by a telegram or a letter from the hon. member. Now the minister should tell us what word he received from the hon. member and why he dismissed this man.
I was not minister when this happened and I have no information from the department regarding it, but if I had been minister and an hon. member from any riding had made the same complaint
You mean a Liberal member ?

Well, a Liberal member, if my hon. friend
APRIL 16, 1903i
(Mr. Hughes, Victoria) prefers it-that a foreman was acting in the same way as this man was doing in employing unworthy and improper men instead of good men 1 certainly think he would have been asked to give an explanation. In reference to these matters, as far as I am concerned, we always ask for a report from the engineer as to the facts. But on such a request as this I think any hou. gentleman in this Committee will admit that it is worthy of investigation and if the statements are found to be correct, this man ought to be dismissed.

Probably it is not reasonable to expect from the present hon. Minister of Public Works an explanation respecting these matters.. I think the letter which I read to-night was dated before the hon. minister assumed control of the department of Public Works, but we are fortunate in having in the House his predecessor in office and if that hon. gentleman would not be revealing any departmental secrets we would like to know from him if he issued any instructions respecting the dismissal of men in British Columbia.

So many things have passed through my brain since that time that I cannot really remember the details of that story. All I remember is that I heard that name ' Sinclair ' before. There was something that was not agreeable to my hon. friend (Mr. Galliher). The facts I believe are these : Sinclair was appointed in 1901 on the recommendation of my hon. friend. Assuming that he was still persona grata, the resident engineer, Mr. Keefer employed him to continue the work he had been employed upon. Some friction took place. I speak from memory. I asked Mr. Keefer what was the matter and the next thing I heard was that Mr. Keefer had dispensed with the services of Mr. Sinclair, no doubt at the request of my hon. friend here, ns he said. The appointment of foremen gives the minister a lot of trouble and I am very glad to have got rid of that.

I think it is due to the Committee that the hon. member (Mr. Galliher), who claims to have been instrumental in dismissing this officer, should give us the reasons why he was not satisfied with his conduct. Who were the men that Sinclair was employing and who were the men the hon. member wished to have him employ ?

If I remember aright, I left the whole matter in the hands of the resident engineer which is the only safe way to do. British Columbia is very far away and unless the minister gives the resident engineer as much of his confidence as is possible, trouble will certainly come. If I had any friendly advice to offer the hon. Minister of Public Works I would urge
him to strengthen the hands of the resident engineers as much as he is able to do. Otherwise, improper parties will be forced upon him.
Hear, hear.

Well, politics are politics, as my hon. friends know. Members of parliament are exposed to a grent deal of pressure and to save them from that pressure the best thing to do is to instruct the resident engineers to employ only safe and honourable men. I have always endeavoured to do so and Mr. Keefer has carried out my orders with great care in the past.
He is a very competent officer.
He is a good officer. He was recommended to me by hon. members on both sides of the House.

I would like to ask the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tnrte) and also the present hon. Minister of Public Works what the custom is in relation to the treatment of these engineers. For instance, if the hon. member for Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Galliher) wished to dispense with the services of Mr. Sinclair was it not his bounden duty to communicate with the Minister of Public Works and then let the minister issue his instructions to the resident engineer. I understand from a statement made by the hon. member himself that he simply took the bull by the horns and compelled Mr. Keefer to dismiss this man.
No, not by any means.
If the hon. exMinister of Public Works is responsible for this dismissal it is not much .wonder that the right hon. Prime Minister asked for his resignation.

I would not like to discuss that question again now ; We will see later on. As to the Sinclair business it did not take place as my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes, Victoria) believes it did. There was a complaint made to me
When was that complaint made-recently ?

No, there was a complaint made before he was dismissed. There was a complaint that something was going wrong, that Sinclair did not act agreeably to my hon. friend (Mr. Galliher) in the appointment of men. I simply referred the matter to Mr. Keefer giving him to a very large extent carte blanche, and the next thing I heard was that Mr. Keefer had dispensed with the services of Sinclair and appointed another man in his place.

Mr. Keefer seems to have placed the responsibility of the dismissal upon the shoulders of the ex-Minister of

Public Works. He had no option apparently if tlie letter I read is correct. I have no doubt it is as Mr. Keefer has just received such a high certificate of character from the former head of the department. Mr. Keefer, in his letter, states that he received instructions from Ottawa that he was to take his instructions from the hon. member for Yale and Cariboo. Did the hon. exminister give those instructions to Mr. Keefer ?

As I remember the facts, speaking of Sinclair alone, I simply referred the complaint of my hon. friend (Mr. Galliher) to Mr. Keefer and the next thing I heard was that the services of Sinclair had been dispensed with. I would be very glad indeed to have the whole of the correspondence brought down but I think it will confirm the facts as I state them now. In other words there was an agreement between my hon. friend and Mr. Keefer as to dispensing with the services of Sinclair. I do not believe that I gave an order to dismiss Sinclair. I simply referred the whole thing to Mr. Keefer.

I have asked for an explanation from the hon. member for the riding as to what persons Sinclair was employing that were objectionable, why they were objectionable and what ones were sought to be employed and why they were sought to be employed.

I have already stated that on that river that is being cleared there were a number of new settlers who had gone in who had taken up homesteads and who were hewing out homes for themselves along that river. I thought, as I believe any fair-minded man in this House would think, that where money was expended the benefit of that money should go to those settlers along the river rather than to men in towns who have no landed interest there and who have no homesteads there.
What town ?
The town of Salmon Arm.
What is the population of that place ?
I could not tell the hon. gentleman. He has travelled through there, I have no doubt. It is a very small town in the west around which you cannot find a few hangers on.
A town of four houses ?

[DOT] My hon. friends need not be so much exercised over this because Sinclair is no friend of theirs. I thought they might be under the impression that some friend of theirs was being very hardly dealt with.
No, it is injustice to a poor Liberal.
The hon. member (Mr. Galliher) recommended him ?
I recommended him myself in 1901. The whole crux of the case is right here; that man was not a foreman for 1902.
The ex-minister suggests that in order to refresh his memory the whole correspondence should be brought down.

I did not mean that, but if the hon. gentleman wants the correspondence I suppose there is no objection to it, but the item should be carried all the same.
Some resolutions reported.
By command of His Excellency I lay on the Table correspondence in relation to the German tariff.

I wish to make a remark as to certain correspondence that was read to-day by the Finance Minister, and some of which was three or four years old. It seems extraordinary that this correspondence was not brought down to the House before today. I think it was asked for several times, and yet the first we heard of it was when the Minister of Finance read it to-day.
I do not think that Is treating this House with the courtesy to which it is entitled.
I have no recollection of the correspondence having been asked for. If any motion were made and passed for an Order of the House for that correspondence, it certainly would have been brought down.

A motion was not made, but a request was made across the floor of. the House.
The MINISTER OF - FINANCE. It does not always follow as a rule that it is wise to bring down correspondence on matters of that sort. However, I have no recollection of any motion having been passed or of any request even having been made. I expected to be able to lay this correspondence on the Table at 6 o'clock, but I may say that I have sent a copy of it to the leader of the opposition.

In 1901 I asked for this correspondence, and last year the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) moved for it in the House and there was quite a debate upon it, but it was refused by the government.
im

That is another matter. If a motion was made and refused, of course it was refused for good reasons. It is not always wise to bring down correspondence, especially in matters of an international character; but I think considering all the circumstances, that it is open to debate whether any good purpose would have been served by bringing down the correspondence. The time was spent in an effort to come to an understanding with the German government, but I am not sure that it would have been promoted by bringing down the papers and broadening the scope of the discussion.
But this correspondence is four years old.
There is plenty of correspondence over four years old that has never been brought down.
And never will.
And never will, as my kon. friend says, for a good and sufficient reason, that the public interest would not be advanced by bringing it down.

I do not think that reason could be advanced in this case. The correspondence was read to-day, and there is no .*justifiable reason why it should not have been placed before the House. It all stopped years ago.

My kon. friend is mistaken in saying that it stopped years ago. He will see from the papers which I have laid on the Table that it extended down to a very recent date. It began years ago, but did not stop years ago.
On motion of the Minister of Finance, House adjourned at 10.50 p.m.

Fbiday, April 17, 1903.
